# Agent companion part 1 of 4: Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Shadowing

Part 1 of 4 of the agent companion for the kafka-migration-shadowing solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Design contract

One entry per rule, in build order: the rule, where to look in the target, why the problem requires it, and what it depends on.

### 1. Start the environment

**Rule:** Turn on authentication on both clusters before either accepts its first connection, and name the cluster in every command so no command can reach the wrong side.

**Adapt:** Find how the source and target clusters are configured and how tools connect to them; check that SASL is on from first boot on both sides and that each tool's connection settings say which cluster it reaches.

**The problem.** You need the cluster you migrate from and the cluster you migrate to on one laptop, and both must behave like production clusters. A real source already has a security posture, so a demo with an open broker proves nothing about it. Turning security on later leaves a window where a cluster is open, and breaks every client that connected without credentials at the moment it changes.

**How Redpanda helps.** The target needs no setup beyond its start flags: Redpanda creates the first SCRAM user from `RP_BOOTSTRAP_USER` on first boot, sets `enable_sasl`, puts SASL on both Kafka listeners, makes that user the only superuser, and serves its built-in Schema Registry with HTTP basic auth against the same SCRAM users. The source is Apache Kafka configured the way a secured KRaft cluster is: the bootstrap user added at format time, SASL/SCRAM on every client listener, and the `StandardAuthorizer`. Confluent Schema Registry runs next to it as its own service. See [Configure Authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authentication/).

Two `rpk` helper containers, one per cluster, carry the connection settings for their side as `RPK_*` variables. Every command in this solution is `scripts/stack exec rpk-source rpk ...` or `scripts/stack exec rpk-target rpk ...`, so the command itself says which cluster it reaches. The `rpk` CLI speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the source helper works against Kafka and Confluent Schema Registry for everything except users. No command carries a password: the demo credentials live only in `.env`.

The steps reach a service with `scripts/stack`, for example `scripts/stack logs orders-consumer`. It reads `PLATFORM` from `.env` and runs the same command in the Compose service on Docker Compose or in the Deployment or StatefulSet of the same name on Kubernetes, so each step shows one command for either platform.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Real clusters in a cloud account, such as Amazon MSK and Redpanda Cloud: closest to production, but they cost money and need network access and credentials before you run a single command.
- One `rpk` profile that you switch between clusters: fewer containers, but which cluster a command reaches depends on hidden state, so a command can land on the wrong side.

**In production:** Encrypt every listener, give each application its own credential, and give the link only read-only ACLs on the source, with one group grant for every consumer group you migrate; delete the link's user after the cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: security](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-security).

### 2. Seed the source cluster

**Rule:** Before you migrate, inventory every topic's partition count, cleanup policy, and retention and every subject's schema IDs, because those are what a migration silently breaks, and keep partition counts unchanged until every consumer has moved.

**Adapt:** Find the source cluster's topic configurations and Schema Registry subjects; check partition counts, cleanup policies, retention, the subject naming strategy, and schema IDs against what the target will get.

**The problem.** Migrations fail on the details that are not records. A partition count that changes breaks key ordering. A cleanup policy can silently become `delete`, a retention can grow a disk, and a schema's ID can move. A copy that re-produces records starts each target partition at offset 0, so when the source log starts above 0, every committed offset points at a different record on the target. You need an inventory of each before you migrate, and partition counts must stay unchanged until every consumer has moved.

**How Redpanda helps.** The `rpk` CLI speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the inventory commands on this page, `rpk topic describe -c`, `rpk topic describe -p`, and `rpk registry subject list`, run unchanged against Apache Kafka with Confluent Schema Registry and against the Redpanda cluster you migrate to. See [rpk topic describe](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-topic/rpk-topic-describe/) and [Redpanda Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Kafka's own CLI, such as `kafka-topics.sh --describe` and `kafka-get-offsets.sh`: it works against both clusters through the Kafka API, but it needs a Java runtime and a client config file per cluster, and its output differs from what the target-side tools print.
- Skip the inventory and check the target afterward: less work up front, but with no baseline, a changed partition count or cleanup policy goes unnoticed until a consumer misbehaves.

**In production:** Inventory every topic's partition count and configuration before you migrate, and keep partition counts unchanged until every consumer has moved; if you must change one while the link runs, change it on the source only, because the link keeps each shadow topic's partitions in step with the source's.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: partitions](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-partitions).

Check that each topic's retention on the target covers the migration window plus the consumers' expected backlog before you create the link.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: data retention](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-data-retention).

### 3. Start the shop's workload

**Rule:** Migrate underneath the running application, treat each consumer group's committed offsets as its record of what it has processed, and move clients by changing only their connection settings.

**Adapt:** Find every producer and consumer group on the source; check which connection settings each reads from configuration and what offsets each group has committed.

**The problem.** The migration has to happen underneath a running application. The application runs first and never stops producing until you decide to. The consumer group matters more than the producer: its committed offsets are the application's memory of what it has processed. Losing them means either reprocessing everything or skipping records.

**How Redpanda helps.** The application is a stock franz-go Kafka client, and it stays one. Redpanda implements the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the same `orders-service` image runs against either cluster by changing two environment variables, `BROKERS` and `SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL`, and that is the whole cutover for the client. The cutover in [Move the consumer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-consumer/) is judged on whether the group resumes at the offset it stopped at. See [Kafka Compatibility](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/kafka-clients/) and [Redpanda Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- A stop-the-world cutover, with the application stopped while you copy: the simplest to reason about, but the application is down for as long as the copy takes.
- Dual writes from the application to both clusters: no copy of live traffic, but it needs a code change, the clusters drift whenever one write succeeds and the other fails, and consumer offsets still do not move.

**In production:** Inventory every consumer group on the source before the migration and move the groups one at a time, each excluded from the link's offset sync before it starts on the target, because each group is its own cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: consumer scaling](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-consumer-scaling).

### 4. Grant the shadow link read-only access

**Rule:** Give the replication its own user on the source with read-only ACLs: READ and DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the migrated topics, DESCRIBE and READ on the migrated groups, and DESCRIBE on the cluster, and nothing that writes.

**Adapt:** Find the credential your replication or migration tool uses on the source; check whether it is a superuser and whether any of its ACLs allow a write.

**The problem.** A migration tool holds a credential to your production cluster for as long as the migration runs, which is days or weeks. If that credential is a superuser, a bug or a leaked password can delete topics or write records on the cluster the business still runs on.

**How Redpanda helps.** Shadowing reads the source through the Kafka API, as a consumer would, so it needs only what a consumer needs: `READ` and `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on the topics it copies, `DESCRIBE` and `READ` on the groups whose offsets it copies, and `DESCRIBE` on the cluster to list topics and read ACLs. The link runs inside the target broker as part of Redpanda, so there is no second credential to manage on the target and no separate process to secure. See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Run the link as the source's superuser: no ACLs to work out, but the migration then has more power over the source than any application on it.
- Grant `READ` on every topic: one ACL instead of a prefix, but the link can then read topics the migration has no reason to see.

**In production:** Encrypt every listener, give each application its own credential, and give the link only read-only ACLs on the source, with one group grant for every consumer group you migrate; delete the link's user after the cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: security](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-security).

Check that your source accepts a mechanism the shadow link supports before you plan the migration: SASL/SCRAM, SASL/PLAIN (Redpanda v25.3.2 or later), TLS, or mutual TLS to the brokers, and basic auth or mutual TLS to the registry.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: source authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-source-authentication).

### 5. Create the shadow link

**Rule:** Replicate topics, consumer group offsets, and schemas with one link from the target, filtered to what you migrate, and start each topic from the beginning of its log.

**Adapt:** Find what replicates your topics, offsets, and schemas today; check whether one configuration covers all three and whether the topic filter matches exactly the topics you mean to move.

**The problem.** A live migration has to copy three things that live in different places, the records, the consumer groups' positions, and the schemas, and keep all three current while the source changes. Copying them with separate tools means three things to run, monitor, and keep in step.

**How Redpanda helps.** A shadow link is part of the Redpanda broker: one configuration, created with `rpk shadow create`, replicates topics with their offsets and timestamps, consumer group offsets, the ACLs you filter for, and schemas. It works from any Kafka API-compatible source, including Apache Kafka, Confluent Platform, and Confluent Cloud. In API mode, the link reads the source Confluent Schema Registry over HTTP and imports every subject with its versions and IDs, so records on the wire keep decoding. Shadow topics are read-only until failover, so nothing writes to the target early. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/) and [Migrate Schemas from Confluent Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/migrate-schemas-confluent/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Redpanda Migrator, a Redpanda Connect pipeline between the clusters, which the [Kafka migration solution](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) uses: it writes each record to a new offset on the target and translates committed offsets, and runs as its own process.
- MirrorMaker 2: copies records and translates offsets, but not schemas, and runs on a Kafka Connect cluster.

**In production:** Size the migration from measurements on your own topics: the link's copy rate against the source's produce rate, lag from both clusters over time, and the network path from the target to the source.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: link throughput](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-link-throughput).

Freeze schema deletions on the source during the migration, and expect the target's replicated Schema Registry context to refuse writes until you pause the link's schema sync or delete the link.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: schema validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-schema-validation).

### 6. Verify the replication

**Rule:** Measure replication lag by comparing the high watermarks each cluster reports, never from the replication's own view of the source alone, and confirm schema IDs on the target before any consumer depends on them.

**Adapt:** Find how your migration reports lag; check whether that number comes from the source cluster itself or from the tool's last look at it.

**The problem.** Before you move anything, you need to know the target is a complete, current copy. Two numbers say so: how far behind the target is, and whether every schema a record names is there. Either one read wrong costs data. A lag read from the replication's last look at the source can say 0 while the source holds records the target never received, and a consumer that reaches a record whose schema ID is missing either stops or skips the record.

**How Redpanda helps.** A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, so comparing the clusters is comparing numbers: the same partition, the same offset, the same record. The lag in this step is the difference between the two clusters' high watermarks, each read from its own cluster with `rpk topic describe`. Schema replication in API mode keeps every subject's versions and IDs, including a version registered while the link runs. See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Read the lag from `rpk shadow status`: one command, but the link computes it from its last fetch from the source, so it can read 0 while the source already holds records the link has not fetched.
- Compare record counts: quick, but a count says nothing about whether the records are at the same offsets.

**In production:** Watch the link's task states, measure lag from both clusters' high watermarks, and alert when lag rises for longer than your cutover window.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: observability](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-observability).

Freeze schema deletions on the source during the migration, and expect the target's replicated Schema Registry context to refuse writes until you pause the link's schema sync or delete the link.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: schema validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-schema-validation).

### 7. Move the consumer

**Rule:** Move each consumer group while the producer still writes to the source: stop it, wait until its committed offsets on the target equal the source's, stop syncing that group, then start it on the target.

**Adapt:** Find the order of your cutover runbook; check whether consumers move before producers, and whether anything still writes a group's offsets on the target after its consumers start there.

**The problem.** A consumer that moves to a new cluster has to start at the record it would have read next. Start too early and it reprocesses orders; start too late and it skips them. In most migrations the same record has a different offset on each cluster, so the committed offset has to be translated, and a translation that lands one record off is a silent duplicate or a silent gap.

**How Redpanda helps.** A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, and the link copies committed offsets as they are, so there is nothing to translate: the consumer resumes from its own committed offset. Shadow topics are readable while the link replicates them, so the consumer can move before the producer and read the records the link copies from Kafka. Pausing the group's offset sync is one configuration change on the link. See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Stop the consumer and the producer together, fail over, and start both on the target: one fewer step, but the business stops processing orders for the length of the cutover.
- Translate offsets with a tool that maps source offsets to target offsets, as Redpanda Migrator does: needed when the target's offsets differ from the source's, and it adds the translation as something that can be wrong.

**In production:** Move consumers before producers, stop syncing a group's offsets before its consumers start on the target, and fail over a producer's topics only when both clusters report the same high watermark on every partition.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: cutover order](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-cutover-order).

Inventory every consumer group on the source before the migration and move the groups one at a time, each excluded from the link's offset sync before it starts on the target, because each group is its own cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: consumer scaling](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-consumer-scaling).

### 8. Move the producer

**Rule:** Move the producer last: stop it, fail over only when the target's high watermark equals the source's on every partition, then delete the link so the target's topics and registry take writes, and start the producer there.

**Adapt:** Find the point of no return in your cutover runbook; check what decides that the target has every record before it is made writable, and whether that check reads both clusters.

**The problem.** The producer is the last thing to move, because once it writes to the target, the target is where the data lives. The moment it becomes writable has to be after it holds every record the source does. A target made writable one record early has lost that record, and nothing reports it: the producer's next records fill the same offsets.

**How Redpanda helps.** Failover turns shadow topics into regular, writable topics with one command, and shadow topics refuse writes until then, so nothing can write to the target too soon. Because a shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, proving the target holds every record is a direct comparison: the same high watermark on every partition, each read from its own cluster. Deleting the link after the failover returns the replicated Schema Registry context to read-write. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Fail over when `rpk shadow status` reports lag 0: one command, but that lag comes from the link's last fetch from the source (see [Verify the replication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-replication/#why-this-approach)), so a failover on it can leave the last records on the source only.
- Keep the link and fail over one topic at a time: useful when applications move one by one, at the cost of a cutover that runs for as long as the slowest application takes.

**In production:** Write down the way back for every stage of the cutover before you start, and treat the failover of a producer's topics as the point of no return: a shadow link replicates only into Redpanda, so it cannot carry records back to Kafka.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback).

Run a migration of many topics and groups as waves with an owner and written go/no-go gates for each, and fail over no producer's topics until its consumers have moved and verified.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: migration runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-migration-runbook).

# Agent companion part 2 of 4: Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Shadowing

Part 2 of 4 of the agent companion for the kafka-migration-shadowing solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Design contract (continued)

### 9. Verify the migration end to end

**Rule:** Accept a migration only when the two clusters agree as compared from outside: topic shapes, log start offsets, the last record of every partition by key and timestamp, schema IDs, where every consumer and producer resumed, and that forbidden requests are refused.

**Adapt:** Find the migration's acceptance checks; check whether they compare each partition's last record on both clusters, not only counts, and whether any asserts that an unauthenticated or unauthorized request fails.

**The problem.** Each step's Verify section checked one thing. A migration claims more: that the target holds everything the source held, at the same place, and that the applications carried on from where they stopped. Counts are not enough to prove the first. A producer that starts on the target can write records with the same keys, at the same offsets, as records the cutover lost, and a count or a high watermark comparison then passes. The negative checks matter as much as the positive ones: an unauthenticated client is refused, and the shadow link's user cannot write to the source.

**How Redpanda helps.** A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets and timestamps, so the comparisons are direct. Each partition's log starts at the same offset on both clusters, and the last record the source holds on each partition is on the target at that same offset with the same key and timestamp. A record the producer wrote to the target after the cutover has a later timestamp, so a lost record cannot hide behind a new one. The consumer check compares offset numbers, because the moved consumer must start at exactly the offset the source consumer committed. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/) and [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Compare record counts and high watermarks only: quick, but it misses a producer on the target that wrote over the offsets of lost records.
- Checksum every record on both sides: the strongest proof of the data, but it reads the full history of both clusters, and it still says nothing about offsets or ACLs.

# Agent companion part 3 of 4: Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Shadowing

Part 3 of 4 of the agent companion for the kafka-migration-shadowing solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Production gaps

This solution runs two single-node clusters with demo credentials so that it starts in a minute. Before you reuse the design for a real migration, work through each topic below.

### Brokers and replication

In this solution, each cluster is one broker, so every topic has replication factor 1 on both sides, and the link copies that.

In production, run three or more brokers on the target. The link syncs `replication.factor` with each shadow topic by default, so a topic that ran with replication factor 2 on the source gets 2 on the target. Check every topic with `rpk topic describe` after the link creates it, and raise any that fall below your standard once its topic has failed over and the link no longer manages it. The link runs inside the target brokers, so size the target for the copy as well as for the applications that move to it.

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Link throughput

In this solution, one link copies about fifty records a second across 29 partitions, and the lag stays in the tens of records.

In production, measure before you commit to a cutover date:

- **What to measure.** The source's produce rate per topic in records and bytes, from your existing Kafka or MSK metrics. The link's copy rate and the lag per topic and partition while it copies history, and again once it is level with live traffic. The time the initial copy of retained history takes, which is the size of the retained data divided by the copy rate you measured.
- **Tuning the link.** The fetch settings in `client_options`, `fetch_min_bytes`, `fetch_max_bytes`, `fetch_partition_max_bytes`, and `fetch_wait_max_ms`, decide how much each fetch from the source carries and how long it waits to fill. Change one at a time and measure. The link runs inside the target brokers, so it scales with the target cluster rather than with a process you deploy.
- **Network cost and placement.** The target fetches each record from the source once, directly, so every record crosses the network between the clusters once. When the clusters are in different availability zones, regions, or clouds, that leg can be billed as cross-zone or inter-region transfer, and the initial copy moves your whole retained history. Estimate it from the retained bytes plus the produce rate times the migration window.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

### Security

In this solution, both clusters run SASL/SCRAM over plaintext listeners, the application and Console sign in as the superuser, and both Schema Registries sit behind HTTP basic auth. The Kafka node's controller listener is unauthenticated and bound to the loopback interface, which is why `ANONYMOUS` is in `super.users`. The `shadow` user has the read-only ACLs from [Grant the shadow link read-only access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/grant-shadow-access/) for the one group this solution migrates, `orders-service`.

In production, enable TLS on every Kafka listener and on Schema Registry, and give each application its own credential instead of the superuser. Secure a real Kafka source's controller listeners as its operators already do; never copy this demo's single-node controller setup. Reuse the link's ACL set with your topic prefix or an explicit topic list, plus `DESCRIBE` and `READ` for every consumer group you migrate. The link copies the source's ACLs only when `security_sync_options` lists ACL filters, and this solution sets none; if you add filters, check the target's ACLs after the link starts. The users and their passwords are not replicated: create each application's credential on the target before it moves. Delete the link's user on the source once the last group has moved.

See [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/), [Configure Authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authentication/), [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/), and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Source authentication

In this solution, the link signs in to Apache Kafka with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-256 over plaintext and to Confluent Schema Registry with HTTP basic auth. That registry authenticates users from a file and authorizes nothing, so the link's registry user could write there.

In production, configure the link's `client_options` for your source:

- **Kafka or Confluent Platform with SCRAM.** Keep `scram_configuration` as here, over TLS (`tls_settings.enabled: true`), and keep the read-only ACLs in `scripts/shadow-acls.sh`.
- **Confluent Cloud.** Its brokers take an API key over SASL/PLAIN, so use `plain_configuration` with TLS, and give the key read access to the migrated topics and groups. Its Schema Registry takes a separate API key and secret in `auth_options.basic` of `shadow_schema_registry_api`.
- **Amazon MSK.** The link can connect only when SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 is turned on for the MSK cluster. IAM access control is not supported, and AWS Glue Schema Registry is not supported as a schema source. If your MSK cluster uses only IAM, add SCRAM for the migration or use Redpanda Migrator, which supports IAM, as the [Kafka migration solution](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) shows.
- **Mutual TLS.** Give the link a client certificate and key in `tls_settings`, to the brokers and, separately, to the registry.

Give the link's registry identity read-only access to the subjects you migrate with the registry's own authorization, such as role bindings in Confluent Cloud or Confluent Platform, where it is available. Where it is not, as with the community registry here, treat the credential as a write credential and rotate it after the migration. Whichever mechanism you use, run the read-only proof from [Grant the shadow link read-only access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/grant-shadow-access/) against the real source before you start.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Migrate Schemas from Confluent Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/migrate-schemas-confluent/).

### Partitions

In this solution, the four topics have 12, 6, 8, and 3 partitions, and the link creates each shadow topic with the same count and copies every record to the same partition and offset.

In production, list every topic's partitions, configuration, and log start offsets with `rpk topic describe -c -p` and every subject with `rpk registry subject list` before you start; both work against Apache Kafka, Amazon MSK, and Confluent Schema Registry, so the final verification has a list to match. While a topic is shadowed, change its partition count on the source only. Resize on the target after the topic has failed over and every consumer has moved.

See [Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/manage-topics/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Schema validation

In this solution, the link imports every schema with its source ID into the target's default context, which stays read-only until `make delete-link`, and no broker checks a record's schema ID.

In production, freeze schema deletions on the source for the length of the migration, and register any schema the moved applications need on the source before the cutover, where the link copies it. Delete the link, or pause its Schema Registry sync, right after the last failover, then enable schema ID validation on the migrated topics so that the target refuses a record whose schema it does not hold.

See [Migrate Schemas from Confluent Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/migrate-schemas-confluent/) and [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/).

### Consumer scaling

In this solution, one consumer instance in `orders-service` moves by hand in [Move the consumer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-consumer/).

In production, list every group with `rpk group list` and `rpk group describe`, include them all in the link's `group_filters`, decide the order in which they move, and move each one with the same sequence: stop every instance on the source, wait until the target holds the same committed offsets, exclude the group from the offset sync, then start every instance on the target. Keep the link until the last group and the last producer have moved.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Data retention

In this solution, the topics keep their source retention on the target, because the link syncs `retention.ms`: 7 days, 1 hour, 1 day with compaction, and compaction alone.

In production, check that the synced retention covers the migration window plus the backlog a consumer may still have at the cutover, and that the target has the disk for it, including the retained history the link copies first.

See [Configure message retention](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/disk-utilization/#configure-message-retention).

### Compaction

In this solution, `shop.customer-profiles` is compacted and `shop.inventory-events` is compacted and deleted, but in a run this short compaction removes nothing on the source.

In production, expect history that the source compacted before the link started: the source keeps the offset gaps that compaction left, and a shadow topic keeps the same gaps, because each record is written at its source offset. The high watermarks match, and a committed offset in a compacted range names the same position on both clusters. Compaction runs on each cluster on its own schedule, so an older record for a key can still be on one side after it is gone from the other: compare compacted topics by key and latest value as well as by offsets.

See [Compaction Settings](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/compaction-settings/).

### Cutover order

In this solution, one consumer group moves, the link's whole offset sync pauses, and then one producer moves after every topic fails over at once.

In production, move every consumer group that reads a producer's topics before the producer, because until the producer moves, the source still has every record and each group can go back (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)). For each group:

1. Stop its consumers on the source, and wait until the target holds the same committed offset on every partition.
1. Stop the link copying that group's offsets: add an `EXCLUDE` filter for it to `consumer_offset_sync_options.group_filters` with `rpk shadow update`, rather than pausing the whole offset sync as this solution does, so groups that have not moved yet keep being copied. The link writes a group's offsets whenever the group has no active members on the target, so without the filter a restart of the moved consumers rewinds them to the source's offsets.
1. Start its consumers on the target.

Then, for each producer, pause it, wait until the target's high watermark equals the source's on every partition of its topics, read from both clusters, and fail over those topics with `rpk shadow failover --topic`. Do not fail over on the lag `rpk shadow status` reports: it compares with the link's last view of the source, and can read 0 while the source still holds records the link has not fetched. Records produced in that window exist only on the source after the failover. Repoint the producer only after its topics report `FAILED_OVER`.

The link owns the target's Schema Registry context while it replicates schemas, even after every topic has failed over, so the target refuses new schemas until you pause the link's Schema Registry sync or delete the link. Register every schema the moved applications will need on the source before the cutover, where the link copies it, or plan to delete the link right after the last failover.

See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Rollback

In this solution, nothing is rolled back: the cutover runs forward once and `scripts/verify.sh` checks the result.

In production, plan the way back before each stage, and know which stage you are in:

- **Before any consumer moves.** The link only reads the source. To abandon the migration, delete the link with `rpk shadow delete`; the applications never noticed it. Delete the shadow topics, the copied groups, and the imported schemas on the target, or keep them for the next attempt.
- **After a consumer group moves, before its producers move.** The producers still write only to the source, so the source has every record, and the group's committed offsets there have not moved since you stopped it. Stop the group's consumers on the target and start them on the source again: they resume from the source offsets, and the records they processed on the target are processed again, so this stage relies on the same idempotent processing as the cutover itself. Because the offsets are the same numbers on both clusters, a second attempt needs no cleanup on the target: remove the group's `EXCLUDE` filter and the link copies its offsets again.
- **After a producer's topics fail over: the point of no return.** A failed-over topic cannot return to shadow mode, and records the producer writes there exist only on Redpanda. Shadowing replicates only into a Redpanda cluster, so it cannot copy them back to Kafka. Going back means copying them with another tool, such as Redpanda Migrator or MirrorMaker 2, from Redpanda to Kafka, and then moving consumers back, or accepting that consumers on the source never see them. Build and test that path before the first failover, and fail over in the smallest groups of topics you can, so that a rollback touches as few topics as possible.

Keep the source cluster and its consumer group offsets until every group and producer has moved and `scripts/verify.sh` passes, so each earlier stage stays reversible for as long as possible.

See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/) and [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Migration runbook

In this solution, one person moves one consumer group and one producer in a few minutes.

In production, with dozens of topics and consumer groups owned by different teams, write the runbook before you create the link:

1. **Inventory.** List every topic with its partitions and configuration, every subject, every consumer group with its owner and the topics it reads, and every producer with the topics it writes. Note transactional producers and read_committed consumers (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery)).
1. **Waves.** Group the topics so that each wave holds a set of producers and every consumer group that reads their topics. A group that reads topics of two waves moves with the later one. Give each wave an owner and a window.
1. **Gate: ready to replicate.** Target sized and secured, an Enterprise license applied, `enable_shadow_linking` on, the link's user and its read-only ACLs in place for the wave's topics and groups, and the read-only proof on the source passing. One link can carry every wave: widen its topic and group filters as waves start.
1. **Gate: ready to move consumers.** Lag measured from both clusters' high watermarks within the bound you set for at least a full business cycle, every link task `ACTIVE` in `rpk shadow status`, and the offset and schema checks from `scripts/verify.sh`, adapted to the wave's topics, passing.
1. **Move consumers, one group at a time.** For each group: stop it, wait until the target holds its committed offsets, exclude it from the offset sync, start it on the target, and check that it resumed at the same offsets (`scripts/resumed.sh`, adapted to the group). No-go: any partition that resumed elsewhere. Rollback: move the group back to the source (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)).
1. **Gate: ready to move producers, the point of no return.** Every consumer group of the wave runs on the target, stable and caught up, and each team has signed off. Pause the producers, wait until both clusters agree on every high watermark of their topics, fail those topics over, and repoint the producers.
1. **Close the wave.** Run the full comparison, and keep the source topics until the last wave is done. After the last wave, delete the link, which also returns the replicated Schema Registry context to read-write, then delete the link's user on the source.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

### Idempotency and delivery

In this solution, the source's `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 trimmed records, and every record has the same offset on both clusters, so the consumer resumes at exactly the offset it committed, which [Move the consumer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-consumer/) and `scripts/verify.sh` check. No producer is transactional.

In production, the offsets need no translation: a shadow topic writes each record at its source offset, so trimmed log starts, compaction gaps, and active groups do not move a consumer's position, as they can with a tool that copies records to new offsets. A consumer still reads again any record it processed after its last commit on the source, so keep consumers idempotent, or deduplicating by key, across the cutover. And fail over a producer's topics only when both clusters report the same high watermark on every partition, so no record is left behind on the source.

Test transactional producers and read_committed consumers on a copy of the real topics before the cutover: produce transactions on the source, abort some, and check that a read_committed consumer on the target reads the same committed records and none of the aborted ones.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/) and [Transactions](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/transactions/).

### Dead-letter handling

In this solution, there is no dead-letter topic, and none is needed: the link copies records as they are, and a task that fails reports a state other than `ACTIVE` in `rpk shadow status`.

In production, keep it that way, since a migration that drops records is not a migration. Alert when a task leaves `ACTIVE` or when lag measured from both clusters keeps rising, fix the cause, usually a missing ACL on the source or a full disk on the target, and keep the source until the target has been verified.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

### Observability

In this solution, `make lag` compares both clusters' high watermarks, `rpk shadow status` shows the link's tasks, and each cluster has its own Redpanda Console.

In production, scrape both clusters into your monitoring and chart the difference between the source's and the target's high watermarks per topic. Alert when it stays above a bound you set, the produce rate times the delay you accept, and when any task in `rpk shadow status` leaves `ACTIVE`. Use the link's own lag reading for trends, not for the cutover: it compares with the link's last view of the source, which it refreshes periodically.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/) and [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/).

### Disaster recovery

In this solution, there is no standby: the source is the only other copy, and it is retired after the cutover.

In production, set up Shadowing after the migration so that a second Redpanda cluster stays level with the target, including consumer group offsets and schemas, and can take over if the target fails. The disaster recovery solution, [Survive a cluster outage without reconfiguring clients](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/), builds that setup end to end.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

In this solution, nothing reads the migrated topics except `orders-service`.

In production, enable Iceberg topics on the migrated topics that analytics needs, so the brokers write each record to an Iceberg table with no extra pipeline to run.

See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

# Agent companion part 4 of 4: Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Shadowing

Part 4 of 4 of the agent companion for the kafka-migration-shadowing solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Reference build

How the reference system proves itself. Everything in this section belongs to that system (its seeded data, fixed counts, and local stack): use it to see what each rule protects, not as checks to copy into the target.

### Acceptance checks of the reference

The assertions `make verify` makes against the running reference system.

1. Both clusters answer, and the target reports healthy. Apache Kafka has no health endpoint in the Kafka API, so the source check is a metadata request. Retried because a cluster can be slow to answer for a few seconds after the cutover moves the consumers, with nothing wrong.
2. Authentication is enforced on the source: without credentials, the Kafka listener and the Schema Registry reject the request. (env -u strips the helper's RPK_* credentials.)
3. Least privilege: the shadow link's user can read the source but not write to it. --acks 1 turns off the idempotent producer, so the write reaches the topic ACL check instead of stopping at the cluster-level producer ID request.
4. Every topic exists on the target with the same partition count and the same cleanup policy and retention.
5. Every record the source holds is on the target at the same offset. A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, so each partition's log starts at the same offset on both clusters (shop.orders starts after the 1,200 trimmed records on both), and the target's high watermark is at least the source's: equal when the producer stopped, plus what the producer has written to the target since.
6. Schemas: the same subjects, versions, and IDs on both registries, and shop.orders-value has the version registered after the link started.
7. Consumer group: orders-service has committed offsets on every source partition, the consumer that moved to the target has caught up there, and on every partition it started at exactly the offset the source consumer had committed when it stopped. The offsets are the source's own, so there is nothing to translate.
8. The producer moved too, and carried on: the producer on the target resumed after the highest record number on the source (the producer_seq header of the last record on each partition), so no record number was written twice or skipped.
9. The migration is finished: the shadow link is gone, so the target's topics and Schema Registry take writes.

### Failure modes of the reference

#### Start the environment

If `make up` stops with a container marked `unhealthy`, run `scripts/stack logs <service>`. The usual causes are Docker having less than 6 GB of memory available (the figure on the overview) and one of the host ports already in use (move it with the matching `*_PORT` variable in `.env`, then use your port in the Console URLs of later steps). If a helper or Schema Registry reports `SASL authentication failed`, a data volume holds a user from an earlier run with a different password: run `make clean`, then `make up`.

#### Seed the source cluster

If a subject is missing, run `make schemas` again: registering the same schema twice returns the same ID. If the final table of `make topics` shows a different partition count from the table The four topics, the topic existed from an earlier run with other settings. Delete it with `scripts/stack exec rpk-source rpk topic delete <name>`, then run `make topics` and `make history` again. If `make history` printed a table where the high watermark is above the log start offset, the topic already held records when it ran, and it skipped the trim: start over: run `make clean`, then `make up`.

#### Start the shop's workload

The group is `Stable` with one member; the lag is whatever the service has not read in the last second. If the state is `Empty` or the group does not exist, the service could not connect: `scripts/stack logs orders-consumer` shows whether it was authentication (a changed password in `.env` after the first `make up`) or a missing topic (`make topics` first). If the producer logs `schema for shop.orders-value not found`, run `make schemas`.

#### Grant the shadow link read-only access

If `enable_shadow_linking` prints `false`, run `make shadow-access` again: the target must be healthy for `rpk cluster config set` to apply. If the ACL list is empty, the script failed before it granted anything; run `scripts/stack exec rpk-source bash /scripts/shadow-acls.sh` to see the error.

#### Create the shadow link

If `make link` reports that the link already exists, the link from an earlier run is still there and still replicating: run the Verify command instead of creating it again. If you edited `scram_mechanism` and `make link` reports `When setting SCRAM configuration, must provide username, password, and mechanism`, write it as `SCRAM-SHA-256`, with hyphens. If the topics never appear, run the Verify command of [Grant the shadow link read-only access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/grant-shadow-access/): without the five ACLs the link signs in but lists no topics.

#### Verify the replication

Both add up to 1200, the trimmed history from [Seed the source cluster](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/seed-source/): the target's copy starts where the source's log starts, not at 0.

If the target's sum is 0, the link has not fetched yet: wait five seconds and run the command again. If `make lag` prints `no shop.* topics on the target yet`, run `make link`.

#### Move the consumer

Every row says `yes`: the first offset the consumer processed on Redpanda is the offset it had committed on Kafka. It is reading shadow topics, which the link still fills from Kafka, so it keeps up with the producer that is still on the source.

If a partition shows `no`, the consumer started on the target before `make wait-offsets` finished. The source still holds every order and its committed offsets, so nothing is lost: in production you would stop the consumer on the target and move it back (see [Production considerations: rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)). In this walkthrough, run `make clean` and start again from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/start-environment/).

#### Move the producer

An empty list, with only the header row, means the link is gone.

If `make failover` times out waiting for the lag, the producer is still running: run `make stop-producer` again. If `scripts/stack logs producer-target` shows `POLICY_VIOLATION`, the topics did not fail over: run `make failover`, then restart the producer with `make producer-target`.

#### Verify the migration end to end

A failed check names what it compared. The likely ones: `the source's last record on every partition` fails when the topics failed over before the link had copied the last records; those records are now only on the source, and a failover cannot be undone, so run `make clean` and start again (in production, that is the loss the high watermark wait in `make failover` prevents), `started at the offset the source consumer had committed` fails when the target consumer started before `make wait-offsets` finished, and `the shadow link has been deleted` fails if you skipped `make delete-link`.

## The problem

A Kafka cluster carries a shop's order flow: a Go service produces, a consumer group processes every order, and Confluent Schema Registry holds the contracts. Moving to Redpanda cannot mean stopping producers, replaying history, or losing where each consumer left off.

- **One link, inside the target.** The Redpanda cluster pulls the topics, the consumer group offsets, and the schemas from Kafka itself, so there is no migration process to deploy, size, or keep running between the clusters.
- **Every record keeps its offset.** A shadow topic holds each record at the offset it has on Kafka, so a consumer moves with the offsets it already committed, untranslated.
- **Nothing writes to the target too soon.** Shadow topics refuse writes until you fail them over, so the cutover has one point of no return, and you choose when.
- **The same tool afterwards.** After the shop runs on Redpanda, the same feature keeps a standby cluster for disaster recovery.

You create one shadow link on Redpanda while the application writes to Kafka. The consumer moves first and resumes at the exact offset it stopped at, then the producer moves, and the target holds every record the source did, at the same place.

## What the system must do

- Replicate a live, SASL-secured Kafka cluster's topics, records, consumer group offsets, and Confluent Schema Registry schemas to Redpanda with one shadow link and a read-only source user
- Keep every record at its original offset and every schema at its original ID, including a schema registered mid-migration
- Measure replication lag from both clusters' high watermarks, and know why the link's own lag reading is not enough to fail over on
- Move a consumer group to Redpanda with its committed offsets untranslated, then fail over, delete the link so the target's Schema Registry takes writes, and move the producer so it carries on its numbering
- Prove the migration lost nothing, by checking the last record of every partition on both clusters

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Turn on authentication on both clusters before either accepts its first connection, and name the cluster in every command so no command can reach the wrong side. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/start-environment/))
2. Before you migrate, inventory every topic's partition count, cleanup policy, and retention and every subject's schema IDs, because those are what a migration silently breaks, and keep partition counts unchanged until every consumer has moved. (from [Seed the source cluster](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/seed-source/))
3. Migrate underneath the running application, treat each consumer group's committed offsets as its record of what it has processed, and move clients by changing only their connection settings. (from [Start the shop's workload](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/start-workload/))
4. Give the replication its own user on the source with read-only ACLs: READ and DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the migrated topics, DESCRIBE and READ on the migrated groups, and DESCRIBE on the cluster, and nothing that writes. (from [Grant the shadow link read-only access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/grant-shadow-access/))
5. Replicate topics, consumer group offsets, and schemas with one link from the target, filtered to what you migrate, and start each topic from the beginning of its log. (from [Create the shadow link](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/create-shadow-link/))
6. Measure replication lag by comparing the high watermarks each cluster reports, never from the replication's own view of the source alone, and confirm schema IDs on the target before any consumer depends on them. (from [Verify the replication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-replication/))
7. Move each consumer group while the producer still writes to the source: stop it, wait until its committed offsets on the target equal the source's, stop syncing that group, then start it on the target. (from [Move the consumer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-consumer/))
8. Move the producer last: stop it, fail over only when the target's high watermark equals the source's on every partition, then delete the link so the target's topics and registry take writes, and start the producer there. (from [Move the producer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-producer/))
9. Accept a migration only when the two clusters agree as compared from outside: topic shapes, log start offsets, the last record of every partition by key and timestamp, schema IDs, where every consumer and producer resumed, and that forbidden requests are refused. (from [Verify the migration end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/))

## Adapt

Inspect the target repository before changing it. Answer each item with what you found there.

- [ ] Rule 1: Find how the source and target clusters are configured and how tools connect to them; check that SASL is on from first boot on both sides and that each tool's connection settings say which cluster it reaches.
- [ ] Rule 2: Find the source cluster's topic configurations and Schema Registry subjects; check partition counts, cleanup policies, retention, the subject naming strategy, and schema IDs against what the target will get.
- [ ] Rule 3: Find every producer and consumer group on the source; check which connection settings each reads from configuration and what offsets each group has committed.
- [ ] Rule 4: Find the credential your replication or migration tool uses on the source; check whether it is a superuser and whether any of its ACLs allow a write.
- [ ] Rule 5: Find what replicates your topics, offsets, and schemas today; check whether one configuration covers all three and whether the topic filter matches exactly the topics you mean to move.
- [ ] Rule 6: Find how your migration reports lag; check whether that number comes from the source cluster itself or from the tool's last look at it.
- [ ] Rule 7: Find the order of your cutover runbook; check whether consumers move before producers, and whether anything still writes a group's offsets on the target after its consumers start there.
- [ ] Rule 8: Find the point of no return in your cutover runbook; check what decides that the target has every record before it is made writable, and whether that check reads both clusters.
- [ ] Rule 9: Find the migration's acceptance checks; check whether they compare each partition's last record on both clusters, not only counts, and whether any asserts that an unauthenticated or unauthorized request fails.

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

The cluster you leave is Apache Kafka: one KRaft node (`source`) with Confluent Schema Registry (`source-registry`). The cluster you move to is a single Redpanda broker (`target`). Both run SASL/SCRAM authentication and ACLs from the first boot. The shop's application, a Go producer and the `orders-service` consumer group built on the franz-go Kafka client, works against Kafka until you move it.

- **`source` and `source-registry`**: four `shop.*` topics with different partition counts and cleanup policies, four Avro subjects, and the `orders-service` consumer group. The `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 records that retention already removed, as on a cluster that has run for months, so its offsets do not start at 0.
- **`producer`**: a Go service that writes one Avro record every 20 ms to the four topics, in the Schema Registry wire format, and stamps each record with its number in a `producer_seq` header.
- **`orders-consumer`**: the Go service `orders-service`, a consumer group on `shop.orders` that commits offsets every second.
- **The shadow link**: created on `target` with `rpk shadow create` from `config/shadow-link.yaml`. It signs in to Kafka as the `shadow` user, which has read-only ACLs, and copies the four topics with their offsets and timestamps, the committed offsets of `orders-service`, and every schema with its ID.
- **`target`**: holds the four topics as shadow topics, read-only until the cutover fails them over. Its copy of `shop.orders` starts at the same offset as Kafka's.
- **`orders-consumer-target` and `producer-target`**: the same two images, started against the target during the cutover with only their connection settings changed.
- **Redpanda Console**, one per cluster, signed in as the superuser.

### Data flow

Left to right:

1. The producer looks up the ID of each topic's schema in the Confluent Schema Registry and writes Avro records to the four `shop.*` topics on Kafka. The `orders-service` group consumes `shop.orders` and commits offsets to `__consumer_offsets`.
1. The shadow link runs inside the target broker. It signs in to Kafka as `shadow`, fetches every partition of the four topics, and writes each record at the offset it has on Kafka, with its key, headers, and timestamp.
1. The same link copies the committed offsets of `orders-service` every five seconds, as the same numbers, because the offsets mean the same records on both clusters. An offset is capped at the target partition's high watermark until the records reach the target, and it is written only while the group has no active members on the target.
1. It also polls the source registry over HTTP and imports each schema version under its source ID into the target's built-in Schema Registry.
1. At the cutover the consumer stops on Kafka, its offsets reach the target, and the same image starts on Redpanda. The producer stops, the topics fail over once both clusters hold the same records, the link is deleted, and the producer starts on Redpanda.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A migration that cannot stop the business has four hard requirements. The applications must move without a rewrite. Every record must keep meaning the same thing, which for Avro means keeping its schema ID. Every consumer must resume at the record it would have read next. And the target must not take a write until it holds everything the source does. Redpanda meets each of these:

- **Your clients move as they are.** Redpanda speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the shop's stock franz-go clients keep their consumer groups, keyed partitioning, compaction, and Avro wire format, and moving them changes `BROKERS` and `SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL` and nothing else. See [Kafka Compatibility](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/kafka-clients/).
- **Records, offsets, and schemas replicate in the broker.** Shadowing is part of Redpanda: one link copies topics with their offsets, consumer group offsets, and schemas from any Kafka API-compatible source, with nothing to run between the clusters. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).
- **Offsets need no translation.** A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, so a committed offset names the same record on both clusters. See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).
- **Schema IDs survive.** In API mode, the link imports every version from Confluent Schema Registry under its source ID into the Schema Registry built into the broker. See [Migrate Schemas from Confluent Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/migrate-schemas-confluent/).
- **The target is read-only until you say so.** Shadow topics refuse writes until failover, so the cutover's point of no return is one command you run when the clusters agree. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/).

## Acceptance

The target is done when every rule holds and you can cite the evidence from the target itself: a configuration value, a code path, a test, or a measured result. The reference build's numbers do not transfer.

- [ ] Rule 1 holds (Start the environment).
- [ ] Rule 2 holds (Seed the source cluster).
- [ ] Rule 3 holds (Start the shop's workload).
- [ ] Rule 4 holds (Grant the shadow link read-only access).
- [ ] Rule 5 holds (Create the shadow link).
- [ ] Rule 6 holds (Verify the replication).
- [ ] Rule 7 holds (Move the consumer).
- [ ] Rule 8 holds (Move the producer).
- [ ] Rule 9 holds (Verify the migration end to end).
- [ ] Every Adapt item is answered, and any rule that does not apply to the target is recorded with the reason.
