## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

A game simulator produces `GameEvent` records to two topics. Three consumers read them: a Go leaderboard service that totals each player's score and publishes it to a compacted topic that a small dashboard reads, a Redpanda Connect pipeline that writes match history to Postgres, and a Go achievements service that detects streaks and wins and publishes them back to Redpanda. Redpanda Console shows every schema-backed record decoded.

- **Game simulator** (Go, franz-go): deterministic event stream, idempotent producer, admin API to burst load or inject a poison record.
- **`game.player-events`** and **`game.match-events`**: the two source topics, keyed by `player_id` and `match_id`.
- **Schema Registry**: holds the `GameEvent` Protobuf schema as subjects `<topic>-value` with `BACKWARD` compatibility.
- **Leaderboard service** (Go): consumer group `leaderboard`, one in-memory total per player, publishes the absolute total to `game.leaderboard` after every score change, scales to three instances.
- **`game.leaderboard`**: a compacted topic keyed by `player_id`. Compaction keeps the newest total per player, so the topic is the leaderboard.
- **Leaderboard dashboard** (Go): reads `game.leaderboard` from the start with no consumer group and serves the live top 10 over server-sent events on a fixed port.
- **Redpanda Connect**: consumer group `connect-history`, decodes with Schema Registry, flattens the `oneof`, inserts into Postgres, routes failures to `game.player-events.dlq`.
- **Achievements service** (Go): consumer group `achievements`, per-player state kept in memory because every player lives on one partition and saved to the compacted topic `game.achievements.state` so a restart picks it up, produces to `game.achievements`.
- **Redpanda Console**: decodes Protobuf records with the same schemas.

### Data flow

Left to right:

1. The simulator looks the `GameEvent` schema up in Schema Registry (it never registers one; the contract is created in [Register the schemas](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/register-schemas/)) and produces every event about a player to `game.player-events`, keyed by `player_id`, and every match lifecycle event to `game.match-events`, keyed by `match_id`.
1. Three consumer groups read `game.player-events`.
1. The `leaderboard` group adds each `score_changed` delta to the player's total and publishes that total to `game.leaderboard`, a compacted topic keyed by `player_id`. The dashboard reads that topic from the start and serves the top 10.
1. The `connect-history` group, a Redpanda Connect pipeline, decodes each record through Schema Registry, flattens it, and inserts it into Postgres. A record it cannot decode goes to `game.player-events.dlq` with the error attached.
1. The `achievements` group folds each player's events into a small in-memory state, produces `achievement_unlocked` events to `game.achievements`, and saves the state to `game.achievements.state`, a compacted topic it reads back whenever it is assigned partitions.
1. The dashed `leaderboard-v2` service runs only in [Scale, restart, and replay the consumers](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/scale-and-replay/): the leaderboard image with a corrected scoring rule, in its own group, replaying `game.player-events` from the first record into `game.leaderboard.v2` while the live board stays untouched.
1. Console decodes the Protobuf topics with the same schemas; the state topic holds plain JSON. On the dead-letter topic it decodes whatever still carries a registered schema ID and shows the raw bytes and the `error` header for anything else, which is what you want when you inspect a poison record.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A live leaderboard puts four demands on the system that carries game events. Match traffic arrives in bursts, and the board has to keep up with them. Each player's events have to be applied in order. The leaderboard, the achievements service, and match history read the same events at their own pace, and a scoring bug has to be fixable by replaying the season. And a small studio team has to run all of it. Redpanda meets each of these:

- **Built for bursts.** Redpanda is written in C++ and designed for high throughput with low tail latency on modest hardware, so a burst of match events is appended and fanned out without a bigger cluster to absorb it. See [Redpanda differentiators](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/get-started/intro-to-events/#redpanda-differentiators).
- **One binary to run.** The broker and [Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/) are one binary with no external dependencies, so the whole broker side here is one container, and Console and Redpanda Connect decode Protobuf records with no extra service to run.
- **A contract between teams, enforced in one place.** The game client and the backend services share Protobuf schemas through that built-in registry, which refuses an incompatible change before any consumer sees it, as [Register the schemas](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/register-schemas/) shows.
- **Replay without a second system.** Each consumer group keeps its own [committed offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/), so [Scale, restart, and replay the consumers](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/scale-and-replay/) rebuilds the leaderboard into a new topic while the live board keeps serving. The optional Tiered Storage extension on the last step moves old segments of `game.player-events` to object storage, so how far back a replay reaches is a retention setting instead of a disk size. See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/).
- **Sinks without code.** Redpanda Connect decodes, flattens, and [inserts](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/sql_insert/) match history into Postgres, with a dead-letter topic, from one YAML file.

Redpanda speaks the Kafka API, so the Go services are ordinary Kafka clients ([franz-go](https://github.com/twmb/franz-go)) and the partitioning, consumer group, and compaction behavior your team already knows applies unchanged. If you run Kafka or MSK today, [the Kafka migration solution](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) moves a live workload's topics, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda.

# Agent companion part 1 of 3: Query database changes in a lakehouse seconds after they happen

Part 1 of 3 of the agent companion for the cdc-to-lakehouse solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Design contract

One entry per rule, in build order: the rule, where to look in the target, why the problem requires it, and what it depends on.

### 1. Start the environment

**Rule:** Capture from a real database with logical write-ahead logging or row-based binary logging and a replica identity set before the first change, and write Iceberg tables through the cluster's existing Tiered Storage bucket rather than a separate sink.

**Adapt:** Find the source databases' `wal_level`, `binlog_format`, and replica identity settings, and check whether `cloud_storage_enabled`, `iceberg_enabled`, and the catalog properties point at the bucket Tiered Storage already uses.

**The problem.** CDC breaks in production at the database: the write-ahead log level, the replication slot, the binary log format, and what a delete records. A script that produces CDC-shaped events hides all four, so you need two real databases, a broker, an object store, a catalog, and Spark running together on one machine.

**How Redpanda helps.** On the broker, three groups of cluster properties are the whole lakehouse side of this solution: `cloud_storage_enabled` with the bucket and credential properties for the object store, `iceberg_enabled` for the table writes, and `iceberg_catalog_type` with `iceberg_rest_catalog_endpoint` for the catalog. See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/). Iceberg topics write through the cluster's Tiered Storage configuration, so RustFS is not an extra component added for the lakehouse. It is the same bucket and the same credentials Redpanda already uses to offload topic segments.

**Other ways to do this.**

- A synthetic producer that writes CDC-shaped JSON: it starts in seconds with no databases, but it hides the slot, the log format, and the delete behavior that this solution is about.
- Managed cloud databases and object storage: closer to production, but they need cloud accounts, cost money while they run, and are harder to reset between runs.
- A sink connector that writes Iceberg to its own bucket: a common pattern, but it adds a connector runtime and a second set of storage credentials to the stack.

**In production:** Run three or more brokers with replication factor 3, and size them for Iceberg translation, which adds CPU and object store traffic on every partition leader.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: brokers and replication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-brokers-and-replication).

Deploy Redpanda with the Redpanda Operator against a supported object store and your own Iceberg catalog, because RustFS and the test catalog are for development only.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: Kubernetes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-kubernetes).

### 2. Turn the topic into a lakehouse table

**Rule:** Turn Iceberg on for a topic before anything produces to it, because translation starts where the property was set, and use `value_schema_latest` only when every producer writes one shape you keep in step with the registered schema.

**Adapt:** Find the topics meant to land in a lakehouse; check whether they held records before the Iceberg mode was set, and whether the producers that share a topic write more than one shape.

**The problem.** A lakehouse table needs a schema for every record. The usual way to supply one is to frame each record with a schema id, which every producer then has to do. That is correct when many producers write many schema versions to one topic, but here the capture pipelines write one shape of plain JSON.

**How Redpanda helps.** The table is a topic property. In `value_schema_latest` mode the pipeline writes plain JSON, and Redpanda resolves the table's layout from the `cdc_orders-value` subject, so there is no `CREATE TABLE` to keep in step with the schema. With `redpanda.iceberg.invalid.record.action` set to `dlq_table`, a record that does not deserialize goes to `cdc_orders~dlq` instead of being dropped. You set the property before the capture pipeline exists, because translation starts where the property was set, not at the beginning of the log. See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/) and [Specify Iceberg Schema](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/specify-iceberg-schema/).

The cost of `value_schema_latest` is that the mode trusts you to keep the pipeline and the schema in step, which is why [schema validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-schema-validation) is one of the production topics.

**Other ways to do this.**

- The `value_schema_id_prefix` mode: correct when many producers write many schema versions to one topic. Every producer must frame its records in the Schema Registry wire format (a magic byte, then the schema's id, then the payload), which pipelines writing one shape do not need.
- A separate Spark streaming job that reads the topic and writes Iceberg: you control the table layout fully, but it is another service with its own offsets, retries, and table definition to keep in step with the schema.

**In production:** Leave `iceberg_target_lag_ms` and `iceberg_catalog_commit_interval_ms` at their one-minute defaults until lag metrics show a need, because every commit is a catalog write and every flush is a new Parquet file.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: Iceberg commit timing](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-iceberg-commit-timing).

Reject records that do not match the registered schema when they are produced, and register a schema change before any pipeline writes the new shape.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: schema validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-schema-validation).

### 3. Capture Postgres changes

**Rule:** Snapshot the table before streaming its change log, give the capture a named replication slot so a restart resumes instead of snapshotting again, and alert on the slot, because the database cannot reclaim log the slot has not acknowledged.

**Adapt:** Find the change data capture configuration; check whether it snapshots before streaming, whether its replication slot is named, and whether anything alerts on the log the slot retains.

**The problem.** A lakehouse table that starts at the moment you deployed the pipeline is not a copy of the table, so it cannot answer questions about orders placed last year. A capture that loses its place in the database's log on restart has to take a second snapshot to catch up.

**How Redpanda helps.** The capture is a process, not a cluster. The Redpanda Connect `postgres_cdc` input creates and holds the named slot, takes the snapshot, and then streams the log, all in one input. The pipeline in this step is one container reading one configuration file, and its `redpanda` output writes straight to the broker. See [postgres_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/postgres_cdc/).

The pipeline snapshots before it streams (`stream_snapshot: true`), and the snapshot is what makes the first query answer questions about past orders. The slot is named (`slot_name: cdc_to_lakehouse_orders`) rather than left to a generated name. A named slot is the pipeline's bookmark in the write-ahead log: Postgres keeps it across restarts, so a pipeline that goes down and comes back resumes where it stopped instead of taking a second snapshot.

That bookmark has a cost. Postgres keeps every log segment a slot has not acknowledged, so while the pipeline is down the write-ahead log keeps growing until it fills the disk, which is why the slot appears under [observability](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-observability) in the production topics. You can cap that with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, but a slot that falls behind the cap is invalidated, and the pipeline then has to start over with a new snapshot. A new snapshot cannot report rows deleted while the pipeline was down, which [backfill and re-snapshot](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-backfill-and-resnapshot) covers.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Debezium on Kafka Connect: a reasonable choice if you already operate Kafka Connect, but it means running a JVM cluster with its own internal topics and REST API. The [overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/#if-you-already-run-kafka-connect) compares the two.
- Polling queries on an `updated_at` column: they need no access to the log, but they miss hard deletes and every intermediate state between polls.

**In production:** Encrypt every connection, give each pipeline a database account limited to what capture needs (replication, `SELECT` on the captured tables, and `RELOAD` for the MySQL snapshot's read lock), and read every credential from a secrets store.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: security](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-security).

Rebuild into a new topic and table when a pipeline has to snapshot again, because a snapshot cannot report the rows deleted since the last change the pipeline delivered.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: backfill and re-snapshot](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-backfill-and-resnapshot).

Treat the table as an at-least-once change log: deduplicate in the query or on the way in, because a restart can write a batch twice.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery).

### 4. Shape the change events

**Rule:** Flatten each change into one row before it reaches the lakehouse, with the operation as a word, a literal source, the database's log position, a capture timestamp, and money as exact decimal text, never floating point, and log full rows for tables whose deleted values you need.

**Adapt:** Find the mapping between the capture and the table; check whether rows arrive nested in an envelope, whether they carry a source and a log position, whether any money column becomes a float or double, and the replica identity of each captured table.

**The problem.** A change data capture (CDC) connector's raw output is not shaped for a table. Some connectors wrap each change in an envelope: the row before the change, the row after it, the source metadata, and a one-letter operation code. In a lakehouse table every nested object in that envelope becomes a struct column, and every query starts by unpacking it. Others put the row in the message body and the operation and log position in metadata, which a table does not keep unless something copies them into columns. By default Postgres also writes only the primary key of a deleted row to the write-ahead log, so the change event has `order_id` and nothing else. The lakehouse then records that order 4 was deleted without recording what it was.

**How Redpanda helps.** The mapping is part of the pipeline, not a separate stage. The transformation is a Bloblang `mapping` processor in the same Redpanda Connect configuration file as the input and the output, so there is one thing to deploy and one place the event's shape is defined. See [mapping](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/processors/mapping/). The `postgres_cdc` input already sends the row as the message body, with the operation and the log sequence number in metadata, so the mapping copies those into columns. The `op` field takes the input's `operation` value, a word such as `insert` or `delete`, and renames the snapshot's `read` to `snapshot`, because the column is read by people writing SQL. The `source` field is set to a literal, which is what lets the MySQL pipeline in [Capture MySQL changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-mysql-changes/) write to the same table. The `position` field keeps the database's own log coordinate, so you can trace a row back to the write-ahead log; it is empty on snapshot rows. The `captured_at` field is the pipeline's clock, and it is the column that answers how far behind the lakehouse is.

Reconstructing current state orders the changes by topic offset instead. Offsets follow the order the database applied the changes only under four conditions the pipeline sets:

- Every change to one order shares a key, and so a partition.
- The pipeline runs one processing thread (`threads: 1`), because more threads process batches in parallel.
- The output sends one batch at a time (`max_in_flight: 1`), because the default of 256 lets batches race each other to the broker.
- The output writes idempotently (`idempotent_write: true`, which requires `acks` set to `all` and one produce request in flight per broker, both the defaults), so a retried request cannot land after a later one.

Adding partitions to the topic later moves keys to new partitions and breaks the guarantee for the rows that move.

For deletes, the table in this solution sets `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`, so Postgres logs the whole row. It is not free: every update and delete writes the full old row to the log.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Land the raw envelope and flatten it later with a scheduled SQL or Spark job: you keep the original event, but you add a second table, a job, and a lag between the two.
- Keep the default replica identity and find a deleted row's values in its earlier changes: the log stays smaller, but every query that needs those values joins the table to itself.

**In production:** Log full rows only for the tables whose deleted values you need, because `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` and `binlog_row_image=FULL` write the whole old row on every update and delete.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: source database and capture](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-source-database-and-capture).

Keep `order_id` as the key and size partitions for the change rate, because changes to one row stay in order only within one partition.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: partitions](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-partitions).

### 5. Query the lakehouse with Spark

**Rule:** Keep the lakehouse table an append-only change log and give analysts current state through one shared view: take the newest change per row and drop rows whose newest change is a delete, which also collapses at-least-once duplicates.

**Adapt:** Find the jobs and queries that turn changes into current state; check whether each analyst writes the window query by hand, whether anything rewrites rows in place, and whether they take the newest change per row key.

**The problem.** A lakehouse table that mirrored current state would have to support row-level updates and deletes. That means a job that applies every change to the table as an update or a delete, and a window during which the table disagrees with the database. Delivery from the capture is also at least once, so a restart can write the same change twice.

**How Redpanda helps.** Nothing in this step talks to Redpanda. Spark asks the REST catalog for `lakehouse.redpanda.cdc_orders`, gets a metadata pointer, and reads Parquet files straight out of RustFS, exactly as it would for a table some batch job had written. That is the whole argument for Iceberg topics: the streaming system's output is a table in the format every query engine already reads, so the analysts need no access to the broker and no knowledge that Redpanda exists. The table is an append-only change log, not a copy of the source table: Redpanda writes new Parquet files and never rewrites old ones, and each reader decides what current means. See [Query Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/query-iceberg-topics/).

The cost is that current state is a query, so this step writes it once, as a view, rather than leaving every analyst to reconstruct it. The view numbers the changes per row newest first, keeps the first, and drops the rows whose newest change is a delete. It partitions by `source` as well as `order_id`, because the second storefront's database, which you capture in [Capture MySQL changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-mysql-changes/), numbers its orders from 1 too. It orders by `redpanda.offset` rather than `captured_at`, because `captured_at` has second precision, and the insert and the update from the previous step can land in the same second. The offset follows the order the database applied the changes under the four conditions in [Shape the change events](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/shape-events/). The same view is the deduplication that the at-least-once delivery in [Capture Postgres changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-postgres-changes/) makes necessary: a replayed change produces a second row with the same values at a later offset, and taking the newest change per row keeps one of them. A replay re-sends a contiguous run of changes in their original order, so the newest row per order is still that order's last change. It also casts `total` to `DECIMAL(10,2)` once, so no reader can sum it as a floating-point number.

**Other ways to do this.**

- A current-state table kept by a scheduled `MERGE INTO` from the change log: the usual production choice once the log is large, because readers no longer scan every change, but you run the job, and the table lags the database between runs. Keep the view as the definition the merge has to agree with.
- A streaming job that writes Iceberg row-level deletes: the table holds current state without a schedule, but readers pay to apply the delete files, and the table needs regular compaction.

**In production:** Decide who compacts the table and who owns the current-state view or merge, because Redpanda writes, commits, and expires snapshots but does not compact files or build current state.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: analytics and lakehouse](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-analytics-and-lakehouse).

### 6. Capture MySQL changes

**Rule:** Write the changes from every source database into one table with a literal `source` column, and reconstruct rows by source and primary key together, because separate databases reuse the same ids.

**Adapt:** Find tables fed by more than one database; check that each row records its source and that current-state and deduplication queries partition by source as well as primary key.

**The problem.** The analysts ask about orders, not about which database an order happens to live in. But both storefront databases number their orders from 1, so combining their rows by `order_id` alone mixes up different orders.

**How Redpanda helps.** One output, one topic, one table, two inputs. The second pipeline reads MySQL with the `mysql_cdc` input and writes to the topic the first one writes to, and the broker's translation task does not care how many producers there are. There is nothing to reconcile, and adding a third database is a third pipeline file. Everything else is the same as [Capture Postgres changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-postgres-changes/): the pipeline shape, the topic, the schema, and the table do not change when the source database does. See [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/).

The `source` column is what makes one table safe. Each pipeline's mapping sets it to a literal, so a query can separate the two sources whenever it needs to. The reconstruction query in [Query the lakehouse with Spark](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/query-with-spark/) partitions by `source` and `order_id` rather than `order_id` alone.

**Other ways to do this.**

- One table per database, combined in a `UNION ALL` view: it keeps the sources apart, but each new database means a new table, a new view definition, and queries that must know the list.
- Remapping ids at capture time so they are unique across databases: it avoids a second key column, but it rewrites the database's own keys, so a lakehouse row no longer matches its source row directly.

**In production:** Keep every CDC position somewhere durable and alert before it can be lost, because a lost position forces a re-snapshot, and a re-snapshot leaves the rows deleted in the meantime alive in the lakehouse.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: state and checkpoints](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-state-and-checkpoints).

Log full rows only for the tables whose deleted values you need, because `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` and `binlog_row_image=FULL` write the whole old row on every update and delete.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: source database and capture](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-source-database-and-capture).

# Agent companion part 2 of 3: Query database changes in a lakehouse seconds after they happen

Part 2 of 3 of the agent companion for the cdc-to-lakehouse solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Design contract (continued)

### 7. Verify the pipeline end to end

**Rule:** Prove the pipeline with two invariants, the topic's high watermarks equal the lakehouse table's row count and the current-state view holds exactly the rows and values each source holds now, because the quiet failures leave every service healthy and only the data disagrees.

**Adapt:** Find the existing checks on the pipeline; check whether any compares the topic with the table and the current-state rows with the source rows, value by value, or whether each reports only its own service's health.

**The problem.** A solution that ends at a working query has not proved anything. The interesting failures in this pipeline are quiet: a change never leaves the database because the replication slot stalled, an event reaches the topic but not the table because the schema did not match, or a restart writes a duplicate. Each of those leaves the stack looking healthy and the data disagreeing, so the data is the test.

**How Redpanda helps.** The count that would normally be hardest to trust is the lakehouse one, because it usually comes from a sink connector with its own offsets, its own retries, and its own dead-letter queue to reconcile. Here the table is written by the broker that holds the topic, so the only thing between the topic's offsets and the table's rows is the translation task, and the records it cannot translate land in one table you can query, `cdc_orders~dlq`. See [Troubleshoot Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-troubleshooting/).

Two invariants have to hold. The sum of the topic's partition high watermarks equals the Iceberg table's row count, so nothing was lost between the topic and the table. The `orders_current` view holds exactly the rows each database holds now, with the same order id, customer, status, and total to the cent, so nothing was lost, duplicated, reordered, or rounded between the database and the view. The script checks the second one by reading every row from each database and from the view and comparing them as text. The database's own row count is not expected to equal the event count: Postgres holds 5 orders after 8 change events, because the table is a log of changes, not a copy of the rows.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Per-service health checks and lag metrics: they catch a stopped container or a growing backlog, but each reports only its own service, so a change lost between services passes every check.
- Row counts alone: they are cheap at any size, but a wrong status or a total rounded through a double passes them. On a large table, compare counts and per-column checksums instead of every row.

**In production:** Monitor translation lag, dead-letter records, the replication slot's size, and each pipeline's output, and reconcile the source row count against the reconstructed table on a schedule.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: observability](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-observability).

Alert when records reach the `cdc_orders~dlq` table and decide per topic whether to keep or drop them, because a record the schema rejects never reaches the main table.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: dead-letter handling](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-dead-letter-handling).

## Production gaps

This solution runs one broker, one RustFS container, and two single-node databases with no authentication, so that it starts in a few minutes. Before you build a pipeline like this against production databases, work through each topic in this section.

### Brokers and replication

This solution runs one broker in `dev-container` mode with `--memory 1G` and replication factor 1. Iceberg translation runs on the partition leader, so it shares the broker's one core with everything else the broker does.

Run three or more brokers with replication factor 3, for `cdc_orders` and the `cdc_checkpoints` topic alike. Size the cluster for Iceberg translation rather than assuming spare capacity: each translating partition adds CPU on its leader and requests to the object store. Iceberg topics and Tiered Storage are Enterprise features: this stack runs them on the 30-day trial a new cluster starts with, and a production cluster needs a Redpanda Enterprise license, in addition to the license the CDC inputs need in Redpanda Connect.

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/), [Tune Performance for Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-performance-tuning/), and [Redpanda Licenses and Enterprise Features](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/get-started/licensing/overview/).

### Security

This solution uses plaintext everywhere. The broker and the catalog accept unauthenticated connections, and the databases and RustFS use fixed local credentials from `.env`.

Enable TLS and SASL on the broker. Give each change data capture (CDC) pipeline a database account whose only privileges are the ones capture needs: replication and `SELECT` on the captured tables, plus `RELOAD` for the MySQL snapshot's read lock. Use IAM roles or scoped keys for the object store, and authenticate the REST catalog with `oauth2`, `bearer`, or `aws_sigv4`. Keep the CDC credentials out of the pipeline file: read them from a secrets store.

See [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/) and [Use Iceberg Catalogs](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/use-iceberg-catalogs/).

### Source database and capture

This solution sets `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` on the Postgres `orders` table and runs MySQL with `binlog_row_image=FULL`, so a delete event carries the values the row held. Postgres keeps the pipeline's position in the named replication slot `cdc_to_lakehouse_orders`. The MySQL snapshot takes `FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK` on a two-row table, which is over before you notice it.

Decide the replica identity and the binary log row image per table, because each one adds the full old row to the log for every update and delete. Alert on the replication slot's retained log in Postgres: the database cannot reclaim log a slot has not acknowledged, so a stopped pipeline fills the disk. If you cap it with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, Postgres invalidates a slot that falls behind the cap, and the pipeline can only start over with a snapshot, which cannot report the rows deleted in the meantime: those rows stay live in the lakehouse as ghost rows. Keep the MySQL binary log for longer than the longest pipeline outage you plan to recover from, for the same reason. Schedule the first MySQL snapshot of a large table in a maintenance window, because the read lock it takes is global. When you change a captured table's columns, change the schema and the mapping with it, as the schema drift extension on the last step shows: an added column is silently left out, and a changed type sends every change to the dead-letter table.

See [postgres_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/postgres_cdc/) and [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/).

### Backfill and re-snapshot

This solution snapshots each table once, on a fresh stack, into an empty topic. A pipeline has to snapshot again whenever it has lost its place: the Postgres replication slot was dropped or invalidated by `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, the MySQL checkpoint is gone or points at a binary log file MySQL has already purged, or a snapshot was interrupted before it finished. A snapshot reads the rows that exist, so a row deleted while the pipeline had no position never gets a delete event, and the current-state view keeps it as a live ghost row forever.

Treat a re-snapshot as a reload, not a catch-up:

1. Stop the pipeline and drop its position: the replication slot in Postgres, or, for MySQL, the pipeline's `checkpoint_key` in `cdc_checkpoints`, by producing a tombstone for that key with `rpk topic produce -Z`.
1. Create a new topic, such as `cdc_orders_v2`, with the same Iceberg settings and schema subject, and point the pipeline's output at it. Redpanda writes it as a new table.
1. Start the pipeline. It snapshots into the new topic and streams from the new position.
1. When the new table has caught up, repoint `orders_current` at it, and delete the old topic, which also drops its table while `redpanda.iceberg.delete` is `true`.

Analysts keep reading the view throughout, and the old table stays correct until you switch. For a large table, raise `snapshot_batch_size` (Postgres) or `snapshot_max_batch_size` (MySQL), raise `max_parallel_snapshot_tables` when Postgres snapshots many tables, size the topic's partitions for the snapshot burst, and schedule the MySQL snapshot in a maintenance window, because it takes a global read lock to fix its starting position. Prevent the need where you can: alert on slot lag before `max_slot_wal_keep_size` invalidates the slot, and keep the MySQL binary log longer than the longest outage you plan to recover from.

See [postgres_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/postgres_cdc/) and [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/).

### Partitions

This solution gives `cdc_orders` one partition, keyed by `order_id`. Every change to one order stays in order because it lands in that one partition, with the pipeline settings [Shape the change events](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/shape-events/) lists keeping the batches in order.

Size partitions for the change rate before the first change arrives, and keep the key. Ordering per row holds only within a partition, and an update that overtakes its insert produces a table that reconstructs to the wrong state. Adding partitions later moves keys to other partitions, so a row's next change can get a lower offset than its last one in the old partition; rebuild into a new topic, as [backfill and re-snapshot](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-backfill-and-resnapshot) describes, rather than adding partitions to a live CDC topic.

See [Sizing Guidelines](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/sizing/).

### Schema validation

This solution registers a JSON schema for `cdc_orders-value`, and Redpanda uses it to lay out the table in `value_schema_latest` mode. Nothing stops a producer writing a record that does not match it: the record goes to the dead-letter table instead.

Once more than one pipeline or schema version writes the topic, encode records in the Schema Registry wire format with the Redpanda Connect `schema_registry_encode` processor, switch the topic to `value_schema_id_prefix`, and enable schema ID validation, so a record without a registered schema is rejected at produce time. Register a schema change before the pipeline that writes it: Redpanda caches the latest schema for `iceberg_latest_schema_cache_ttl_ms`, five minutes by default.

See [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/) and [Specify Iceberg Schema](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/specify-iceberg-schema/).

### Iceberg commit timing

This solution sets `iceberg_target_lag_ms` and `iceberg_catalog_commit_interval_ms` to 10 seconds, the lowest commit interval Redpanda accepts, so a change is queryable in the lakehouse within seconds. Both default to one minute.

Start from the defaults. A tighter lag trades query freshness for many small Parquet files and more catalog commits, and small files make every query engine slower until something compacts them, which Redpanda does not do (see [analytics and lakehouse](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-analytics-and-lakehouse)). Lower the lag only for the topics whose readers need it, and watch translation lag and file counts when you do.

See [Tune Performance for Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-performance-tuning/).

### Consumer scaling

Nothing in this solution consumes `cdc_orders` through the Kafka API: the lakehouse write is the broker's own work, and Spark reads object storage.

Iceberg translation costs no consumer group, and the topic still serves streaming readers. Applications that need the changes as a stream read it in their own consumer groups without affecting the table.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Data retention

This solution leaves default retention on a one-partition topic, with Tiered Storage writes on.

The Iceberg table outlives the topic's retention: data written to Iceberg stays queryable after the records age out of the topic. Set the topic's retention for the streaming consumers, and keep the table as the history. Deleting the topic drops its table while `redpanda.iceberg.delete` is `true`, which is the default, so set it to `false` on any topic whose table must survive the topic.

See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/) and [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

### Idempotency and delivery

The pipelines' `redpanda` output batches 50 events or one second, sends one batch at a time (`max_in_flight: 1`), and writes idempotently (`idempotent_write: true`, with `acks` at `all`), and each pipeline runs one processing thread. Those settings keep a producer retry from duplicating or reordering a batch, which the current-state view depends on, because it orders changes by offset. They do not make the pipeline exactly-once: on a restart, `postgres_cdc` resumes from the replication slot's position and `mysql_cdc` from its checkpoint, so changes delivered after the last acknowledged position are written again, in their original order.

CDC is at-least-once, so the table is an append-only log that can hold duplicates. Deduplicate in the query, as the [`orders_current` view](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/query-with-spark/) already does by taking the newest change per row, or on the way in, and make every reader tolerate a repeat. Keep the ordering settings when you tune for throughput: more pipeline threads or batches in flight let changes to one row reach the topic out of order.

See [Idempotent producers](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/produce-data/idempotent-producers/).

### State and checkpoints

In this solution, Postgres holds the `postgres_cdc` position in the replication slot on the database server. MySQL has no server-side cursor, so `mysql_cdc` keeps its binary log position in the `binlog_position` cache resource, a `redpanda` cache that writes it to the compacted `cdc_checkpoints` topic, so a restart resumes from the last acknowledged position.

A lost position is worse than a slow restart. With a `memory` cache, a restarted MySQL pipeline has no position, so it takes a fresh snapshot under a global read lock and writes every row again. A Postgres slot invalidated by `max_slot_wal_keep_size` forces the same. A snapshot cannot emit deletes, so any row deleted while the position was lost has no delete event, and the current-state view shows it as live forever.

Keep the checkpoint topic replicated like any other topic, with a `checkpoint_key` per pipeline, or use another durable cache, such as `redis` or `aws_dynamodb`. Alert on the slot's retained log before it reaches `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, and on MySQL binary log retention shorter than your longest outage. When a position is lost anyway, rebuild as [backfill and re-snapshot](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-backfill-and-resnapshot) describes instead of snapshotting into the existing table.

See [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/), [redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/caches/redpanda/), and [Caches](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/caches/about/).

### Dead-letter handling

This solution leaves `redpanda.iceberg.invalid.record.action` at `dlq_table`, the default, so a record the schema cannot deserialize goes to a `cdc_orders~dlq` table. The verify script checks that the table does not exist.

Alert on the `redpanda_iceberg_translation_dlq_files_created` metric, query the dead-letter table when it moves, and decide per topic whether an invalid record should be kept for inspection or dropped.

See [Troubleshoot Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-troubleshooting/).

### Observability

This solution checks the pipeline by hand: `rpk topic describe`, `make dlq`, a Spark query, and the verify script.

Turn those checks into monitors. Alert on Iceberg translation lag and the dead-letter metric, on the replication slot's size in Postgres (an unconsumed slot fills the disk), and on the Redpanda Connect pipelines' own output metrics. Reconcile each source table against the current-state view periodically, as the verify script does row by row, or with counts and per-column checksums on a large table, because the quiet failures leave every service healthy and only the data disagrees.

See [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/) and [Troubleshoot Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-troubleshooting/).

### Disaster recovery

This solution has no recovery path: one broker and one bucket, and the Iceberg files are the only copy of the table.

The table's files live in object storage, with that store's own durability, and the topic can be shadowed to a second cluster. Choose which of the two you recover from: the topic replays, but the second cluster writes its own Iceberg table.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

This solution runs one Spark container that reads the table through the test REST catalog, and an `orders_current` view over the change log. Nothing compacts the table, which is fine for a few dozen rows.

The broker writes the Parquet files, commits each snapshot to the catalog, and expires old snapshots on its own schedule, five days by default, which also bounds time travel. The rest of the table's upkeep is yours:

- Compact small files. Every translation interval writes new Parquet files, so a busy or low-lag topic accumulates many small ones, and every query engine slows down reading them. AWS Glue and Databricks compact Iceberg tables automatically; otherwise schedule a Spark compaction job, such as the Iceberg `rewrite_data_files` procedure.
- Remove orphan files, such as data files from failed writes, with the Iceberg `remove_orphan_files` procedure, if your catalog does not.
- Own current state. Keep the view as the definition of current state, and once the change log is large, add a scheduled `MERGE INTO` a current-state table that the view's logic defines, so readers stop scanning every change.

Choose the catalog for the platform the analysts already use. AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Open Catalog, and GCP Lakehouse are supported integrations. Glue must be in the same AWS account and region as the cluster. Unity Catalog compacts through predictive optimization, which you enable in the workspace, and the cluster needs `iceberg_disable_snapshot_tagging` set to write to it. Apache Polaris and other REST catalogs have been tested but are not regularly verified. Give each cluster its own namespace if more than one cluster writes to the catalog.

See [Tune Performance for Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-performance-tuning/), [Use Iceberg Catalogs](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/use-iceberg-catalogs/), and [Query Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/query-iceberg-topics/).

### Kubernetes

This solution runs on Docker Compose, or on Kubernetes with the Redpanda Operator through `make k8s-up`, with RustFS and the catalog as one service each. RustFS is here for development and evaluation only: it is not a supported object store for production Tiered Storage.

Deploy Redpanda with the Redpanda Operator, as `kubernetes/redpanda.yaml` does, and point it at a supported object store (Amazon S3, Azure ADLS, or Google Cloud Storage) and your own Iceberg catalog instead of RustFS and the test catalog.

See [Deploy Redpanda for Production in Kubernetes](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/kubernetes/k-production-deployment/) and [Use Iceberg Catalogs](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/use-iceberg-catalogs/).

# Agent companion part 3 of 3: Query database changes in a lakehouse seconds after they happen

Part 3 of 3 of the agent companion for the cdc-to-lakehouse solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Reference build

How the reference system proves itself. Everything in this section belongs to that system (its seeded data, fixed counts, and local stack): use it to see what each rule protects, not as checks to copy into the target.

### Acceptance checks of the reference

The assertions `make verify` makes against the running reference system.

1. Every piece of the stack is up: the broker, Console, the object store, the Iceberg REST catalog, and the source databases.
2. The cluster is configured for Iceberg topics against the REST catalog.
3. The topic writes to Iceberg from the schema, and the schema is registered.
4. The databases hold what the steps left them holding: the seeded orders (five in Postgres, two in MySQL), plus one insert and minus one delete from scripts/change-orders.sh.
5. The change events reached the topic. Five snapshot rows plus three changes from Postgres, and two snapshot rows plus three changes from MySQL when that pipeline has been started too.
6. Redpanda wrote the Iceberg files into the object store and registered the table with the catalog.
7. The lakehouse agrees with the topic, change for change, and with each database, row for row. The counts come from one Spark query (sql/queries.sql, tag=summary); the current rows come from the orders_current view (tag=view), which the script creates or replaces first so it also runs on a stack where the query step was skipped.
8. Nothing failed to translate: Redpanda creates a <topic>~dlq table for records it cannot write, so the absence of that table is the check. The catalog answers 404 for a table that does not exist, so any other status (an error, or no answer) fails the check instead of passing it.

### Failure modes of the reference

#### Start the environment

If `make up` stops with a container marked `unhealthy`, run `scripts/stack logs <service>`. The two usual causes are:

- Docker has less than 8 GB of memory available. Redpanda fails to allocate `--memory 1G`, or MySQL is killed during its first start. Give Docker more memory.
- A host port is already in use. Move it with the matching `*_PORT` variable in `.env`.

If `make up` reports that `createbucket` did not complete successfully, run `scripts/stack logs createbucket`. The catalog and the broker never start until the bucket exists.

If `make k8s-up` times out, it names the wait that failed. Run `kubectl -n cdc-to-lakehouse get pods` to see which pod is not ready, then `scripts/stack logs <service>`. A pod stuck in `Pending` usually means the kind node has less CPU or memory than the Prerequisites ask for.

#### Turn the topic into a lakehouse table

No namespaces, and that is the correct answer at this point. Setting the topic property creates nothing: Redpanda creates the `redpanda` namespace and the `cdc_orders` table in it when it translates the first record, which is what [Capture Postgres changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-postgres-changes/) produces. If `curl` reports a refused connection, the catalog is not running: run `make status`, then `scripts/stack logs catalog`. If `make topic` fails with a topic already exists error, the topic exists from an earlier run of `make topic`; move on. If `make schema` fails, check that the file you registered is valid JSON Schema draft-07 with a `$schema` keyword, which is a hard requirement.

#### Capture Postgres changes

If the high watermark is 0, read the pipeline's log with `make cdc-logs`. A message about a license means the key in `REDPANDA_LICENSE` is invalid or expired; on Kubernetes, fix it in `.env` and run `make k8s-up` again to update the Secret. A message about `wal_level` means the `postgres` service's `command` in `docker-compose.yml` lost `-c wal_level=logical`; compare it with the Complete source in [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/). A message that `orders` does not exist means Postgres found an existing data volume and skipped `postgres/init.sql`: run `make clean`, then repeat the steps from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/). If the slot exists but is `active = f`, the pipeline died after creating it; the log says why.

#### Shape the change events

If the delete event has `null` in `customer_id`, `total`, and `status`, the table does not have `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`: the setting is in `postgres/init.sql`, which only runs on a fresh volume, so run `make clean`, then repeat the steps from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/). If the command waits without printing, fewer than three change events have reached the topic. It returns as soon as they arrive and gives up after 30 seconds; if it gives up, read the pipeline's log with `make cdc-logs`.

#### Query the lakehouse with Spark

Five rows, matching the five the database holds: the four seeded orders that were not deleted, plus the one the insert created, with the status the update gave it. The query is a plain `SELECT` from the view, ordered by source and order id. If the command prints nothing, `scripts/lakehouse.sh` hid Spark's error. See it by running the query directly: `scripts/stack exec spark /opt/spark/bin/spark-sql -S -e 'SELECT * FROM lakehouse.analytics.orders_current'`. A view not found error means the view was never created: run `make lakehouse-view`. A table not found error means nothing has translated yet: run `make wait-lakehouse ROWS=8`, and if it times out, run `make dlq`. A connection error to `rustfs` or `catalog` means that service is down: run `make status`, then `scripts/stack logs <service>`.

#### Capture MySQL changes

Five rows from MySQL and eight from Postgres, in one table, each with the time of its newest change. If the MySQL rows do not arrive, `make cdc-logs` shows the pipeline's output: an access denied message means the replication grants in `mysql/init.sql` did not run, which happens on a reused volume: run `make clean`, then repeat the steps from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/). A message about the binary log means the `mysql` service's `command` in `docker-compose.yml` lost `--log-bin` or `--binlog-format=ROW`; compare it with the Complete source in [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/). If `make changes-mysql` reports that it already ran, the three changes are already applied; continue with the next wait.

#### Verify the pipeline end to end

If a count is still short when the script finishes, it has already waited four minutes for the table, so the shortfall is not lag: run `make dlq`, and read `make cdc-logs` for the pipeline that is short. If a count is short by a whole snapshot (five Postgres rows or two MySQL rows), the snapshot did not translate, which means the topic filled up before `redpanda.iceberg.mode` was set on it: run `make clean` and repeat the steps from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/). If a count is over, a pipeline restart replayed changes (delivery is at least once), or a snapshot ran twice; the row comparisons still pass when the view collapsed them. To get exact counts, run `make clean` and repeat the steps from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/). If a row comparison fails, the message shows both sides: a row only in the view is a delete the view never saw, and a row only in the database is a change still on its way or lost. If the dead-letter check fails, see which records the schema rejected: ``scripts/stack exec spark /opt/spark/bin/spark-sql -S -e 'SELECT * FROM lakehouse.redpanda.`cdc_orders~dlq` LIMIT 10'``.

## The problem

A retailer runs two storefronts after an acquisition: one brand's orders are in Postgres, the other's in MySQL. Finance reconciles them from a day-old export, and support needs one view of all orders within a minute to tell a customer whether a cancellation went through. The usual fix is a change data capture (CDC) connector on Kafka Connect and a sink connector into the lakehouse.

You build it with two moving parts: Redpanda Connect streams both databases' changes into one topic, and Redpanda writes that topic as an Iceberg table that Spark queries. At the end, one Spark view shows the current orders from both storefronts within seconds of each change.

## What the system must do

- Capture inserts, updates, and deletes from Postgres and MySQL with the Redpanda Connect `postgres_cdc` and `mysql_cdc` inputs, without Debezium or a Kafka Connect cluster
- Shape a raw change event into a lakehouse row with one Bloblang mapping, and give the Iceberg table its columns by registering a schema
- Make every change queryable in the lakehouse seconds after it happens, by setting one topic property that makes Redpanda write `cdc_orders` as an Iceberg table itself
- Query the change log in Spark SQL and define a view that gives analysts the current state of both source tables
- Prove that every change the databases made reached the topic and the Iceberg table, and that the current-state view matches each database row for row

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Capture from a real database with logical write-ahead logging or row-based binary logging and a replica identity set before the first change, and write Iceberg tables through the cluster's existing Tiered Storage bucket rather than a separate sink. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/))
2. Turn Iceberg on for a topic before anything produces to it, because translation starts where the property was set, and use `value_schema_latest` only when every producer writes one shape you keep in step with the registered schema. (from [Turn the topic into a lakehouse table](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/enable-iceberg-topics/))
3. Snapshot the table before streaming its change log, give the capture a named replication slot so a restart resumes instead of snapshotting again, and alert on the slot, because the database cannot reclaim log the slot has not acknowledged. (from [Capture Postgres changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-postgres-changes/))
4. Flatten each change into one row before it reaches the lakehouse, with the operation as a word, a literal source, the database's log position, a capture timestamp, and money as exact decimal text, never floating point, and log full rows for tables whose deleted values you need. (from [Shape the change events](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/shape-events/))
5. Keep the lakehouse table an append-only change log and give analysts current state through one shared view: take the newest change per row and drop rows whose newest change is a delete, which also collapses at-least-once duplicates. (from [Query the lakehouse with Spark](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/query-with-spark/))
6. Write the changes from every source database into one table with a literal `source` column, and reconstruct rows by source and primary key together, because separate databases reuse the same ids. (from [Capture MySQL changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-mysql-changes/))
7. Prove the pipeline with two invariants, the topic's high watermarks equal the lakehouse table's row count and the current-state view holds exactly the rows and values each source holds now, because the quiet failures leave every service healthy and only the data disagrees. (from [Verify the pipeline end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

Two operational databases, one streaming pipeline each, and one lakehouse table. Redpanda Connect follows each database's change log and writes a flat event per row change to the `cdc_orders` topic. Because that topic has `redpanda.iceberg.mode` set, the brokers write the topic's records into RustFS as an Iceberg table and commit each new snapshot to an Iceberg REST catalog. Spark reads the table through the same catalog, and Redpanda Console shows the topic and its schema.

- **Postgres** with a `pandashop` database and an `orders` table of five rows: the first storefront's database, with `wal_level=logical` so its write-ahead log can be decoded.
- **MySQL** 8.4 with the same table and two rows: the second storefront's database, with row-based binary logging. Its order ids also start at 1, so every event carries a `source` column that tells the two apart.
- **Redpanda Connect**, twice: one pipeline per database, each with a CDC input, a Bloblang mapping, and a `redpanda` output. Both write to the same topic, and the MySQL pipeline keeps its binary log position in a compacted `cdc_checkpoints` topic.
- **Redpanda** with Tiered Storage, Iceberg topics, and its built-in Schema Registry. It is the broker, and it also writes the table's files and commits its snapshots.
- **RustFS** as the S3-compatible object store, holding both the Tiered Storage segments and the Iceberg table files.
- **An Iceberg REST catalog** (`apache/iceberg-rest-fixture`), which Redpanda commits table snapshots to and Spark discovers tables through.
- **Apache Spark** as the query engine, running `spark-sql` against the catalog.
- **Redpanda Console**, to inspect the topic, its configuration, and the registered schema.

### Data flow

Left to right: an application changes a row in Postgres. Postgres writes that change to its write-ahead log. Redpanda Connect holds a logical replication slot on that log, decodes the change, and the pipeline's Bloblang mapping turns it into one flat event with the operation, the row's values, the change log position, and a capture timestamp. The `redpanda` output writes the event to `cdc_orders`, keyed by `order_id`, one batch at a time with idempotent writes, so every change to one order lands in one partition in the order the database applied them.

From there Redpanda does the work a sink connector would normally do. The topic's `redpanda.iceberg.mode` is `value_schema_latest`, so the brokers read the latest schema registered for the `cdc_orders-value` subject, use it to lay out an Iceberg table, deserialize each record against it, and write Parquet data files into the same RustFS bucket Tiered Storage uses. They commit a new table snapshot to the REST catalog within the lag target: this solution sets 10 seconds, and the default is one minute. A record the schema cannot deserialize goes to a separate `cdc_orders~dlq` table rather than being dropped.

Spark asks the catalog for the table, reads the Parquet files straight out of RustFS, and sees the change log as rows. The MySQL pipeline is the same shape with a different input, and it writes to the same topic, so one table answers questions about both storefronts.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

Getting database changes into a lakehouse usually takes three systems between the database and the table: a change capture service on a Kafka Connect cluster, a Kafka cluster, and a sink connector that writes Iceberg files and commits them to a catalog. Each one is another thing to deploy, size, secure, and debug when a change fails to appear. This solution needs only two moving parts between the databases and the table, Redpanda Connect and the broker, and Redpanda is what makes that possible:

- **The broker writes and commits the Iceberg table.** One topic property turns a topic into an Iceberg table, so there is no sink connector to deploy and no second copy of the data: the Parquet files and the topic's Tiered Storage segments live in the same bucket. You still own table maintenance, such as compacting small files, and the current-state view analysts query; [analytics and lakehouse](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-analytics-and-lakehouse) says who runs what. See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).
- **The table's columns come from the built-in Schema Registry.** Redpanda lays the table out from the latest schema registered for the topic's subject, in the same binary as the broker, so the schema that validates the change events is the one that shapes the table. See [Specify Iceberg Schema](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/specify-iceberg-schema/).
- **CDC is a pipeline, not a cluster.** The Redpanda Connect `postgres_cdc` and `mysql_cdc` inputs read the write-ahead log and the binary log from one process each, with no Kafka Connect cluster. See [postgres_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/postgres_cdc/) and [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/).
- **Tiered Storage is the object store wiring.** Iceberg topics write through the cluster's Tiered Storage configuration: one bucket and one set of credentials. See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/).

The change topic is still an ordinary Kafka topic. Keyed partitioning keeps each order's changes in order, and any Kafka client can read the stream in its own consumer group while Redpanda writes the table. If you run Kafka or Amazon MSK today, the [Kafka migration solution](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) moves a live workload's topics, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda.

## Acceptance

The target is done when every rule holds and you can cite the evidence from the target itself: a configuration value, a code path, a test, or a measured result. The reference build's numbers do not transfer.
