# Agent companion part 1 of 3: Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Redpanda Migrator

Part 1 of 3 of the agent companion for the kafka-migration solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Design contract

One entry per rule, in build order: the rule, where to look in the target, why the problem requires it, and what it depends on.

### 1. Start the environment

**Rule:** Turn on authentication on both clusters before either accepts its first connection, and name the cluster in every command so no command can reach the wrong side.

**Adapt:** Find how the source and target clusters are configured and how tools connect to them; check that SASL is on from first boot on both sides and that each tool's connection settings say which cluster it reaches.

**The problem.** You need the cluster you migrate from and the cluster you migrate to on one laptop, and both must behave like production clusters. A real source already has a security posture, so a demo with an open broker proves nothing about it. Turning security on later leaves a window where a cluster is open, and breaks every client that connected without credentials at the moment it changes.

**How Redpanda helps.** The target needs no setup beyond its start flags: Redpanda creates the first SCRAM user from `RP_BOOTSTRAP_USER` on first boot, and the flags set `enable_sasl`, put SASL on both Kafka listeners, make that user the only superuser, and turn on HTTP basic auth for the built-in Schema Registry against the same SCRAM users. The source is Apache Kafka configured the way a secured KRaft cluster is: the bootstrap user added at format time, SASL/SCRAM on every client listener, and the `StandardAuthorizer`. Confluent Schema Registry runs next to it as its own service. See [Configure Authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authentication/).

Two `rpk` helper containers, one per cluster, carry the connection settings for their side as `RPK_*` variables. Every command in this solution is `scripts/stack exec rpk-source rpk ...` or `scripts/stack exec rpk-target rpk ...`, so the command itself says which cluster it reaches. The `rpk` CLI speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the source helper works against Kafka and Confluent Schema Registry for everything except users. No command carries a password: the demo credentials live only in `.env`.

The steps reach a service with `scripts/stack`, for example `scripts/stack logs migrator`. It reads `PLATFORM` from `.env` and runs the same command in the Compose service on Docker Compose or in the Deployment or StatefulSet of the same name on Kubernetes, so each step shows one command for either platform.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Real clusters in a cloud account, such as Amazon MSK and Redpanda Cloud: closest to production, but they cost money and need network access and credentials before you run a single command.
- One `rpk` profile that you switch between clusters: fewer containers, but which cluster a command reaches depends on hidden state, so a command can land on the wrong side.

**In production:** Encrypt every listener, give each application its own credential, and give the migrator only the ACLs a migration needs, with one group grant for every consumer group you migrate; rotate the migrator's credential after the cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: security](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-security).

### 2. Seed the source cluster

**Rule:** Before you migrate, inventory every topic's partition count, cleanup policy, and retention and every subject's schema IDs, because those are what a migration silently breaks, and keep partition counts unchanged until every consumer has moved.

**Adapt:** Find the source cluster's topic configurations and Schema Registry subjects; check partition counts, cleanup policies, retention, the subject naming strategy, and schema IDs against what the target will get.

**The problem.** Migrations fail on the details that are not records. A partition count that changes breaks key ordering. A cleanup policy can silently become `delete`, a retention can grow a disk, and a schema's ID can move. A source log that does not start at 0 means the target numbers every record differently, so any check that compares offsets as numbers is wrong. You need an inventory of each before you migrate, and partition counts must stay unchanged until every consumer has moved.

**How Redpanda helps.** The `rpk` CLI speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the inventory commands on this page, `rpk topic describe -c`, `rpk topic describe -p`, and `rpk registry subject list`, run unchanged against Apache Kafka with Confluent Schema Registry and against the Redpanda cluster you migrate to. See [rpk topic describe](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-topic/rpk-topic-describe/) and [Redpanda Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Kafka's own CLI, such as `kafka-topics.sh --describe` and `kafka-get-offsets.sh`: it works against both clusters through the Kafka API, but it needs a Java runtime and a client config file per cluster, and its output differs from what the target-side tools print.
- Skip the inventory and check the target afterward: less work up front, but with no baseline, a changed partition count or cleanup policy goes unnoticed until a consumer misbehaves.

**In production:** Inventory every topic's partition count and configuration before you migrate, and keep the counts identical on both sides until every consumer has moved, because offset translation and key ordering depend on matching partitions.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: partitions](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-partitions).

Check that each topic's retention on the target covers the migration window plus the consumers' expected backlog before you start the migrator.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: data retention](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-data-retention).

### 3. Start the shop's workload

**Rule:** Migrate underneath the running application, treat each consumer group's committed offsets as its record of what it has processed, and move clients by changing only their connection settings.

**Adapt:** Find every producer and consumer group on the source; check which connection settings each reads from configuration and what offsets each group has committed.

**The problem.** The migration has to happen underneath a running application. The application runs first and never stops producing until you decide to. The consumer group matters more than the producer: its committed offsets are the application's memory of what it has processed. Losing them means either reprocessing everything or skipping records.

**How Redpanda helps.** The application is a stock franz-go Kafka client, and it stays one. Redpanda implements the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the same `orders-service` image runs against either cluster by changing two environment variables, `BROKERS` and `SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL`, and that is the whole cutover for the client. See [Kafka Compatibility](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/kafka-clients/) and [Redpanda Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- A stop-the-world cutover, with the application stopped while you copy: the simplest to reason about, but the application is down for as long as the copy takes.
- Dual writes from the application to both clusters: no copy of live traffic, but it needs a code change, the clusters drift whenever one write succeeds and the other fails, and consumer offsets still do not move.

**In production:** Inventory every consumer group on the source before the migration and move the groups one at a time, each after its own offset wait, because each group is its own cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: consumer scaling](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-consumer-scaling).

### 4. Grant the migrator least-privilege access

**Rule:** Run the migration tool as its own user with read-only ACLs on the source and prefixed create and write ACLs on the target, including `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on source topics and `READ` on target topics, and put the target Schema Registry in `IMPORT` mode before any schema reaches it.

**Adapt:** Find the credential the migration tool uses; check whether it is a superuser, which ACLs it holds on each cluster, and whether the target registry is empty and in `IMPORT` mode.

**The problem.** A migration tool holds credentials for two clusters at once, one of them production, for days. A superuser would work, and is exactly what you do not want it to run as: a bug or a leaked credential could then write or delete anything on either side. The schemas it copies also carry IDs that every record refers to, so the target must accept those IDs as they are.

**How Redpanda helps.** The ACL model is Kafka's on both sides: a principal, an operation, and a literal or prefixed resource. Kafka's `StandardAuthorizer` and Redpanda enforce the same grants, so one script, `scripts/migrator-acls.sh`, grants the source side on Kafka and the target side on Redpanda with `rpk security acl create`, and `rpk security acl list --allow-principal` shows the result the way an auditor would read it. Prefixed ACLs on `shop.` make the target grant safe for topics the migrator has not created yet. What is specific to the target is its Schema Registry's `IMPORT` mode, one `rpk registry mode set` away. It lets a client register a schema under a specific ID and version instead of the next free one, which is how the migrator keeps the source's IDs. Setting it globally requires an empty registry, one where no schema was ever registered or every schema was hard-deleted, unless you override the check with `--force`, so this step happens before anything reaches the target. See [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/) and [rpk security acl create](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-security/rpk-security-acl-create/).

The source registry is the weak spot. Confluent Schema Registry's basic auth, as configured here, authenticates the users in the file that `schema-registry/start.sh` writes and authorizes nothing, so the `migrator` user could register schemas on the source registry. Per-subject read-only access there needs the registry's own authorization, which [Production considerations: source authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-source-authentication) covers.

Two operations are easy to miss. The first is `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on the source topics. A `READ` grant implies `DESCRIBE` but not `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS`, and without it the migrator consumes records but fails to recreate the topic with its configuration. The second is `READ` on the target topics. Committing a consumer group's offsets is authorized against the group and against every topic the commit names, so the migrator needs it to write the translated offsets of `orders-service`.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Run the migrator as a superuser: no ACLs to work out, but a bug or a leaked credential can change anything on both clusters for the length of the migration.
- Literal ACLs for each topic instead of a prefix: a tighter grant, but every topic added to the source later needs a new grant before the migrator can create it on the target.

**In production:** Encrypt every listener, give each application its own credential, and give the migrator only the ACLs a migration needs, with one group grant for every consumer group you migrate; rotate the migrator's credential after the cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: security](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-security).

Authenticate the migrator to your source the way its other clients do, with SCRAM, IAM, or OAUTHBEARER on the Kafka side and basic auth, OAuth, or mutual TLS on the registry side, and give its registry identity read-only access where the registry can enforce it.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: source authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-source-authentication).

### 5. Start the migration

**Rule:** Move records, topic configurations, schemas, and consumer group offsets with one pipeline while the application keeps writing, keep schema IDs untranslated, and sync group offsets often enough that the cutover waits seconds.

**Adapt:** Find the tools that copy records, topics, schemas, and offsets today; check whether they are separate, whether schema IDs are rewritten, how often offsets sync, and whether a new source topic is picked up without a config change.

**The problem.** A migration moves four kinds of state together: records, topic configurations, schemas, and consumer group offsets. The usual toolbox splits them across tools: a replicator for records, topic configurations, and offsets, and a separate tool or script for schemas. The gaps between them are where a cutover breaks, and all of it has to happen while the application keeps writing.

**How Redpanda helps.** The `redpanda_migrator` input and output are part of Redpanda Connect, so one pipeline carries all four kinds of state. The migrator is a container, a YAML file, and a metrics endpoint, with the same SASL and TLS options as any Connect component. Topic creation copies the source's partition count and the topic settings the target supports, such as `cleanup.policy`, `retention.ms`, and `compression.type`. The `topic_replication_factor` setting overrides the replication factor for a bigger target, and `sync_topic_interval` picks up topics that exist on the source but have no traffic. The migrator runs under the `migrator` user from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/). Everything it does on the target is something that user was granted; if it tried anything else, the broker would refuse. See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/).

Four settings carry the design of this solution. The first is `translate_ids: false` in the output, so the schema ID in every record's first five bytes resolves on the target without rewriting a byte. The second is `consumer_groups` with a ten-second interval, so the offsets of `orders-service` follow the consumer closely and the cutover waits seconds, not minutes; `offset_header` (its default value, written out here) is what makes the translation exact at the cutover. The migrator uses that header only for a group with no active members, which is why the cutover stops the consumer before it waits for the offsets. The third is the `regexp_topics_include` pattern on the input, so a topic added to the source later is picked up without a config change. The fourth is `transaction_isolation_level: read_committed` on the input: the default, `read_uncommitted`, would copy the records of aborted transactions too.

**Other ways to do this.**

- MirrorMaker 2: copies records, topic configurations, consumer group offsets, and ACLs, but not schemas, so you run a second tool for the registry. It runs on Kafka Connect, and by default it prefixes each copied topic with the source cluster's alias unless you configure `IdentityReplicationPolicy`.
- Let the target registry assign its own schema IDs (`translate_ids: true`): the target keeps its own numbering, but the migrator rewrites the schema ID in every copied record, and any system that stored a source ID no longer matches.

**In production:** Run the target on three or more brokers and have the migrator create every topic with the target's replication factor, one in-flight batch per source partition, and topic sync left on.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: brokers and replication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-brokers-and-replication).

Size the migrator from measurements on your own topics: copy rate against the source's produce rate, lag over time, and the network path between the clusters, and add migrator capacity before the backlog grows.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: migrator throughput](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-migrator-throughput).

### 6. Verify the schemas

**Rule:** Preserve every schema's ID and version on the target and sync the registry more often than schemas change, so copied records decode there and a schema registered mid-migration arrives before a record that uses it.

**Adapt:** Find the source registry's subjects and versions; check that the target returns the same ID and version for each and how often the registry sync runs.

**The problem.** Schema IDs are the join between records and their definitions. A consumer, a UI, or a pipeline reads the five-byte prefix of a record's value and asks the registry for that ID. If a migration registers the schemas afresh and the target hands out different IDs, every copied record points at the wrong schema or at none. Every consumer then needs a translation table until the old records age out. Migrations also take days and teams do not stop shipping, so a schema registered on the source mid-migration must reach the target before a record that uses it does.

**How Redpanda helps.** The Redpanda Schema Registry implements `IMPORT` mode, as Confluent Schema Registry does, so the migrator can register a schema under an explicit ID and version. Preserving the IDs (and, for the same reason, the version numbers) makes the copied history usable on the day of the cutover, for your consumers, Redpanda Console, and Redpanda Connect alike. The registry sync runs with `interval: 10s` here (five minutes by default), far more often than schemas change. The `rpk registry` commands expose subjects, versions, and mode, so you can diff them between two clusters. The `rpk topic consume --use-schema-registry` command decodes records the same way an application would, which proves that a copied record decodes, not only that its schema arrived. See [Redpanda Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/) and [Use the Schema Registry API](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-api/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Export and import the registry once, before the copy: a simple one-time job, but a schema registered on the source after the export never reaches the target, and records that use it fail to decode there.
- Point target clients at the source registry until cutover: no schema copy at all, but the target then depends on the cluster you plan to retire.

**In production:** Freeze schema deletions during the migration, migrate every version with its original ID in `IMPORT` mode, and switch the target registry to `READWRITE` as the last step of the cutover.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: schema validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-schema-validation).

### 7. Monitor the migration lag

**Rule:** Gate the cutover on observable conditions, migration lag within a stated bound while traffic runs and at zero before a producer moves, and translated offsets that point at the same records as the source's, and watch the error counters as the audit trail.

**Adapt:** Find what reports the migration's progress; check whether lag per topic and partition is alerted on against a bound derived from the produce rate, and whether the created, committed, and error counters are scraped.

**The problem.** You cannot cut over until the target has every record the source has. While the copy is behind, a consumer moved now would either skip records or wait for them. You also need a record of what the copy did and what it could not do, or a failed topic creation or offset commit goes unnoticed until the cutover.

**How Redpanda helps.** Redpanda Connect exposes every pipeline's metrics in Prometheus format on its HTTP server, and the `redpanda_migrator` components add their own. The input reports `redpanda_lag` per topic and partition. The migrator also reports `redpanda_migrator_topics_created_total`, `redpanda_migrator_sr_schemas_created_total`, `redpanda_migrator_cg_offsets_committed_total`, and their error counterparts. Lag is the migration's progress bar and its safety check at once. The cutover in [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/) waits for two things, and both are visible here: the migrator's lag at zero, and translated offsets that point at the same records as the source's. The counters are the audit trail: how many topic creations, schema registrations, and offset commits the migrator has made, and (from the `_errors_total` series) how many it could not. See [Monitoring](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/guides/monitoring/) and [the migrator's metrics](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/#metrics).

The counters carry `path="root.input"` because the migrator registers its metrics on the input side, although the output drives the schema and group sync.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Compare record counts on both clusters with a script: needs no metrics stack, but it is a snapshot at one moment, and it says nothing about schema registrations or offset commits that failed.

**In production:** Scrape the migrator's metrics, chart `redpanda_lag` by topic, and alert when lag rises for longer than your cutover window or when any migrator error counter moves.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: observability](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-observability).

Alert on the migrator's output errors and on rising lag, because the pipeline retries a failed write and stops on a permanent one instead of dropping records.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: dead-letter handling](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-dead-letter-handling).

# Agent companion part 2 of 3: Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Redpanda Migrator

Part 2 of 3 of the agent companion for the kafka-migration solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Design contract (continued)

### 8. Finish the cutover

**Rule:** Cut over one consumer group at a time: stop the consumer, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets, and start it on the target; then pause the producer, drain to lag 0, and repoint it, which is the point of no return, and switch the target registry to `READWRITE` only after that.

**Adapt:** Find the cutover runbook; check the order in which it stops and starts consumers and producers, whether it compares the records offsets point at rather than the offset numbers, where it names the point of no return and the rollback before it, and when it leaves `IMPORT` mode.

**The problem.** The order of the cutover is the whole design. A consumer started on the target before its offsets arrive starts from `earliest` or `latest`, the two outcomes a migration exists to avoid. A producer that writes to the target while migrated records are still arriving interleaves the two, and records with the same key lose their order. And once a producer writes to the target, the source no longer has every record, so that move is the one you cannot simply undo.

**How Redpanda helps.** Redpanda Migrator translates each committed offset through the record's timestamp and, for a group with no active members, refines it with the source offset it stored in every copied record's `redpanda-migrator-offset` header, so the target offset points at the exact record even though the numbers differ. It commits that offset as an ordinary Kafka client, with `READ` on the group and on the topic. The target's group coordinator hands `orders-service` that offset when the consumer joins, as Kafka's would, so the application changes nothing. The migrator keeps the offsets of every group it migrates current on the target, so you can cut over one consumer group at a time while the source stays authoritative. See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

Stop the consumer first, so its group is `Empty` and its committed offsets are fixed numbers the migrator can translate exactly. Wait for the translation, and only then start the consumer on the target. Move the producer last, and only after the migrator has drained its topics to lag 0. Switch the target registry to `READWRITE` last. Until every producer has moved, the migrator still registers source schemas under their source IDs, which needs `IMPORT` mode. Once producers write to the target, they register new schemas there, which needs `READWRITE`.

**Other ways to do this.**

- A stop-the-world cutover: stop every producer and consumer, wait for lag 0, and start everything on the target. Fewer steps to coordinate, but the whole application is down at once, and every team moves in the same window.
- Start each consumer on the target from a timestamp, with `rpk group seek --to <timestamp>` (plus `--topics` and `--allow-new-topics`, because the group has no commits there yet): no wait for offset sync, but you pick the timestamp by hand, and any gap or overlap means skipped or reprocessed records.

**In production:** Move consumers before producers, pause each producer until the migrator's lag on its topics is 0 before you point it at the target, and treat that repoint as the point of no return.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: cutover order](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-cutover-order).

Write down, for each group and producer, the rollback for every stage of the cutover, and treat repointing a producer at the target as the point of no return, because from then on the source no longer holds every record.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback).

Run a migration of many topics and groups as waves with an owner and written go/no-go gates for each, and do not let any wave repoint a producer until its consumers have moved and verified.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: migration runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-migration-runbook).

Make every consumer tolerate reading a few records again across the cutover, stop each group before it moves so its offsets translate exactly, and test transactional topics and topics with gaps before you rely on their translation.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery).

### 9. Verify end to end

**Rule:** Accept a migration only when the two clusters agree as compared from outside, on topic shapes, record counts, schema IDs, the records each consumer group resumes on, and security posture, including checks that forbidden requests are refused, and never on offset numbers being equal.

**Adapt:** Find the migration's acceptance checks; check whether they compare source and target answers directly and whether any asserts that an unauthenticated or unauthorized request fails.

**The problem.** Each step's Verify section checked one thing. A migration claims more: that the two clusters agree with each other. That means every topic with the same shape, every record, every schema under the same ID, including an order written with a version registered mid-migration, every consumer group resuming on the right record, and the security posture intact on both sides. The comparisons must hold in general, not only on a fresh cluster: offsets differ between the clusters, so a check that compares offset numbers or high watermarks passes only when both logs start at 0. And the negative checks matter as much as the positive ones: an unauthenticated client is refused, and the migrator user cannot write to the source or create topics outside `shop.` on the target.

**How Redpanda helps.** The `rpk` CLI asks both clusters the same questions through the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so most checks compare the source's answer with the target's as strings, whether the cluster runs Kafka or Redpanda. The target's mode is the Redpanda-specific check: `rpk registry mode get` proves that the target left `IMPORT` mode, the mode that let the migrator register every schema under its source ID. See [Use the Schema Registry API](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-api/) and [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/).

The checks are exact because this run is fixed. The producer has stopped, so record counts (high watermark minus log start offset) are fixed numbers. The consumer check compares records by key, not offsets by number. Schemas were registered in a known order, so the IDs are known.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Spot-check a sample of records: quick on a big cluster, but a sample can miss the one topic or partition that did not copy.
- Checksum every record on both sides: the strongest proof of the data, but it reads the full history of both clusters, and it still says nothing about offsets or ACLs.

## Production gaps

This solution runs two single-node clusters with demo credentials so that it starts in a minute. Before you reuse the design for a real migration, work through each of these topics.

### Brokers and replication

In this solution, each cluster is one broker, so every topic has replication factor 1 on both sides, and the migrator copies the source's replication factor because nothing overrides it. The `max_in_flight` setting is 29, one batch per source partition, and `sync_topic_interval` creates a topic on the target even before it carries a record.

In production, run three or more brokers on the target and set `topic_replication_factor: 3` on the `redpanda_migrator` output, so migrated topics get the target's standard even when the source used less. Set `max_in_flight` to the number of partitions you migrate, and leave `sync_topic_interval` on so that empty and low-traffic topics are created too. Run the migrator close to the target cluster: it produces every record with acknowledgments, so produce latency to the target bounds its throughput.

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/) and [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/).

### Migrator throughput

In this solution, one migrator process copies about fifty records a second across 29 partitions, and its lag stays within a few seconds of production.

In production, measure before you commit to a cutover date:

- **What to measure.** The source's produce rate per topic in records and bytes, from your existing Kafka or MSK metrics. The migrator's copy rate and `redpanda_lag` per topic and partition while it copies history, and again once it is level with live traffic. The time the initial copy of retained history takes, which is the size of the retained data divided by the copy rate you measured.
- **Tuning one process.** The `redpanda_migrator` input and output document the settings for high throughput: `partition_buffer_bytes` and `max_yield_batch_bytes` on the input, and `max_in_flight` on the output, up to the number of partitions copied in parallel. Change one at a time and measure.
- **More than one process.** The input balances the source partitions across every process that shares its `consumer_group`, so you can run more migrator processes with the same configuration. Each process also runs the topic, schema, and consumer group syncs. Alternatively, split the topics between separate migrator processes, each with one input and output pair in its own config file and its own `regexp_topics_include` pattern and consumer group, so one team's large topics do not hold up another's. Test the layout you choose on a copy of your workload, including a restart of one process mid-copy.
- **Network cost and placement.** Every record crosses the network twice: read from the source and written to the target. When the clusters are in different availability zones, regions, or clouds, both legs can be billed as cross-zone or inter-region transfer, and the initial copy moves your whole retained history. Estimate it from the retained bytes plus the produce rate times the migration window, and place the migrator where it saves the most, usually in the same zone as the target, since its writes wait for acknowledgment.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/), [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/), and [Monitoring](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/guides/monitoring/).

### Security

In this solution, both clusters run SASL/SCRAM over plaintext listeners, the application and Console sign in as the superuser, and both Schema Registries sit behind HTTP basic auth. The Kafka node's controller listener is unauthenticated and bound to the loopback interface, which is why `ANONYMOUS` is in `super.users`. The `migrator` user has the least-privilege ACLs from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/) for the one group this solution migrates, `orders-service`.

In production, enable TLS on every Kafka listener and on Schema Registry, and give each application its own credential instead of the superuser. Secure a real Kafka source's controller listeners as its operators already do; never copy this demo's single-node controller setup. Reuse the migrator's ACL set with your topic prefix or an explicit topic list, plus `DESCRIBE` on the source and `READ` on the target for every consumer group you migrate: list the same groups in `consumer_groups.include`. With `DESCRIBE` on the cluster the migrator lists every group, including ones such as Confluent Schema Registry's `schema-registry` group, and a listed group it may not describe makes the offset fetch fail for the whole sync, with `GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED` in the migrator's log. Add `sync_topic_acls` and the cluster `ALTER` it needs on the target only if ACLs migrate too. Enable Schema Registry authorization so that the registry grants are as narrow as the Kafka ones, and rotate or delete the migrator's credential on both clusters once the last group has moved.

See [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/), [Configure Authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authentication/), [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/), [Schema Registry Authorization](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-authorization/), and the [migrator's required permissions](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/#required-permissions).

### Source authentication

In this solution, the migrator signs in to Apache Kafka with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-256 over plaintext and to Confluent Schema Registry with HTTP basic auth. That registry authenticates users from a file and authorizes nothing, so the migrator's registry user could write there.

In production, configure the `redpanda_migrator` input for your source:

- **Amazon MSK with IAM access control.** Set `sasl[].mechanism: AWS_MSK_IAM` with `sasl[].aws.region` and credentials (`from_ec2_role`, `role` to assume, or a `profile`), and turn on `tls`. Grant the IAM principal the same operations as the source ACLs in `scripts/migrator-acls.sh`, expressed as `kafka-cluster:` actions in an IAM policy: connect to and describe the cluster, read and describe the topics and their dynamic configuration, describe the groups you migrate, and describe and alter the migrator's own group. Amazon's IAM access control documentation maps each Kafka operation to its action; check the policy with the read-only proofs below.
- **Amazon MSK or Kafka with SCRAM.** Keep `SCRAM-SHA-512` or `SCRAM-SHA-256` as here, over TLS, and keep the ACLs in `scripts/migrator-acls.sh`.
- **OAUTHBEARER.** Set `sasl[].mechanism: OAUTHBEARER` with a `token`. The input sends that one token for each session and does not fetch a new one, so issue a token that outlives the migration window, or plan restarts with a fresh token, and test the behavior when it expires.
- **Confluent Schema Registry or Confluent Cloud.** The input's `schema_registry` block supports `basic_auth` (a Confluent Cloud API key and secret), `oauth`, `jwt`, and `tls` with client certificates. Give that identity read-only access to the subjects you migrate with the registry's own authorization, such as role bindings in Confluent Cloud or Confluent Platform, where it is available. Where it is not, as with the community registry here, treat the migrator's registry credential as a write credential and rotate it after the migration.

Whichever mechanism you use, run the read-only proofs from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/) against the real source before you start: listing topics works, and an idempotent produce and a `--acks 1` produce are both refused.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/) and the [migrator's required permissions](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/#required-permissions).

### Partitions

In this solution, the four topics have 12, 6, 8, and 3 partitions, and the migrator recreates each with the same count and copies every record to the same partition number.

In production, list every topic's partitions, configuration, and log start offsets with `rpk topic describe -c -p` and every subject with `rpk registry subject list` before you start; both work against Apache Kafka, Amazon MSK, and Confluent Schema Registry, so the final verification has a list to match. Keep partition counts identical during the migration: offset translation needs matching counts, and a different count on the target sends keys to other partitions. Resize on the target only after every consumer has moved. The migrator copies every topic setting on its supported list that the source reports, including Kafka's defaults such as `segment.bytes` and `max.message.bytes`, as topic-level overrides on the target, so compare `rpk topic describe -c` on both clusters and remove the overrides you want the target's cluster defaults for.

See [Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/manage-topics/).

### Schema validation

In this solution, schemas are registered on the source, the target registry stays in `IMPORT` mode until the cutover so that every ID is preserved, and no broker checks the schema ID of a record.

In production, freeze schema deletions on the source for the length of the migration, and keep `versions: all` so that consumers pinned to an old version keep working. Migrate in `IMPORT` mode with preserved IDs, return the target to `READWRITE` as the last step of the cutover, then enable schema ID validation on the migrated topics so that the target refuses a record whose schema it does not hold.

See [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/).

### Consumer scaling

In this solution, one consumer instance in `orders-service` moves by hand in [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/).

In production, list every group with `rpk group list` and `rpk group describe`, decide the order in which they move, and move each one with the same sequence: stop every instance on the source, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets, then start every instance on the target. Keep the migrator running until the last group and the last producer have moved.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Data retention

In this solution, the topics keep their source retention on the target: 7 days for `shop.orders`, compaction alone for `shop.customer-profiles`, 1 day with compaction for `shop.inventory-events`, and 1 hour for `shop.alerts`.

In production, check that the target's retention covers the migration window plus the backlog a consumer may still have at the cutover, and that the target has the disk for it.

See [Configure message retention](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/disk-utilization/#configure-message-retention).

### Compaction

In this solution, `shop.customer-profiles` is compacted and `shop.inventory-events` is compacted and deleted, but in a run this short compaction removes nothing before the migrator copies the records, so both topics hold the same number of records on the two clusters and `scripts/verify.sh` can compare the counts exactly.

In production, expect history that the source compacted before the migrator started: the source keeps the offset gaps that compaction left, and the migrator writes the remaining records one after another, so the target's high watermark for that topic is lower than the source's and the same record has different offsets. Compare compacted topics by key and latest value instead, and check each group's translated offsets by the records they point at (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery) for the gap case to test). Compaction runs on each cluster on its own schedule, so an older record for a key can still be on one side after it is gone from the other.

See [Compaction Settings](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/compaction-settings/).

### Cutover order

In this solution, the producer stops after the consumer has moved, the migrator drains, and `scripts/verify.sh` compares the two clusters once.

In production, create each application's user on the target and grant its ACLs there before you move it: the migrator copies no users, and copies topic ACLs only with `sync_topic_acls`, without their `WRITE` grants. Move every consumer group that reads a producer's topics before the producer, because until the producer moves, the source still has every record and each group can go back (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)). Then pause the producer, run the lag check until the migrator's lag on its topics is 0, and only then point it at the target. A producer that writes to the target before the drain finishes interleaves its records with migrated records that are still arriving, so records with the same key can land out of order. If a pause is not acceptable, accept that records produced to the target during the drain can precede migrated records with the same key. Run the comparisons in `scripts/verify.sh` as the acceptance test for each migrated topic and group, and keep the source cluster until they pass for the last one.

See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

# Agent companion part 3 of 3: Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Redpanda Migrator

Part 3 of 3 of the agent companion for the kafka-migration solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Production gaps (continued)

### Rollback

In this solution, nothing is rolled back: the cutover runs forward once and `scripts/verify.sh` checks the result.

In production, plan the way back before each stage, and know which stage you are in:

- **Before any consumer moves.** The migrator only reads the source and writes the target. To abandon the migration, stop the migrator; the applications never noticed it. Delete the copied topics, schemas, and consumer groups on the target, or keep them for the next attempt.
- **After a consumer group moves, before its producers move.** The producers still write only to the source, so the source has every record and the group's committed offsets there have not moved since you stopped it. Stop the group's consumers on the target and start them on the source again with the source connection settings: they resume from the source offsets. Records the group processed on the target after the cutover are processed again, so this stage relies on the same idempotent processing as the cutover itself. The target's committed offsets for the group are now behind, and the migrator never moves a target offset backwards, so delete the group on the target (`rpk group delete`) before you try the cutover again.
- **After a producer writes to the target: the point of no return.** Records it writes exist only on the target, and the migrator copies in one direction. Going back means either copying those records to the source and then moving consumers back as above, or accepting that consumers on the source never see them. Every record the migrator copied carries its `redpanda-migrator-provenance` header and a record written to the target directly does not, so a Redpanda Connect pipeline from the target to the source can copy back only the records without that header. Build and test that pipeline before the cutover, because key order between copied-back records and the source's last records is yours to check. Decide which before you repoint the first producer, and repoint producers in the smallest groups you can, so that a rollback touches as few topics as possible.

Keep the source cluster, its consumer group offsets, and the migrator running until every group and producer has moved and `scripts/verify.sh` passes, so each earlier stage stays reversible for as long as possible.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [rpk group delete](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-group/rpk-group-delete/).

### Migration runbook

In this solution, one person moves one consumer group and one producer in a few minutes.

In production, with dozens of topics and consumer groups owned by different teams, write the runbook before the migrator starts:

1. **Inventory.** List every topic with its partitions and configuration, every subject, every consumer group with its owner and the topics it reads, and every producer with the topics it writes. Note transactional producers and read_committed consumers (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery)).
1. **Waves.** Group the topics so that each wave holds a set of producers and every consumer group that reads their topics. A group that reads topics of two waves moves with the later one. Give each wave an owner and a window.
1. **Gate: ready to copy.** Target sized and secured, migrator ACLs or IAM policy in place for the wave's topics and groups, the read-only proofs pass on the source, target registry in `IMPORT` mode.
1. **Gate: ready to move consumers.** Migration lag within the bound you set (`scripts/lag.sh --check` with your `LAG_BOUND`) for at least a full business cycle, no movement on any `redpanda_migrator_*_errors_total` counter, and the record and schema comparisons from `scripts/verify.sh` passing for the wave's topics.
1. **Move consumers, one group at a time.** For each group: stop it, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets (`scripts/wait-for-offsets.sh`, adapted to the group), start it on the target, and check where it resumed (`scripts/resumed.sh`, adapted). No-go: any partition that resumed on another record. Rollback: move the group back to the source (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)).
1. **Gate: ready to move producers, the point of no return.** Every consumer group of the wave runs on the target, stable and caught up, and each team has signed off. Pause the producers, drain to lag 0, repoint them.
1. **Close the wave.** Run the full comparison, keep the source topics read-only until the last wave is done, then retire them, leave `IMPORT` mode after the last wave, and delete the migrator's credentials.

See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Idempotency and delivery

In this solution, the source's `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 trimmed records, so every copied record has a different offset on each cluster, and the consumer still resumes on the right record, which [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/) and `scripts/verify.sh` check by comparing records, not offsets. No producer is transactional and no topic has been compacted yet.

In production, plan for how the migrator translates an offset. For each committed offset, it reads the record just before it on the source and finds the first target record with that timestamp or later. For a group in the `Empty` state, it then reads that record's `redpanda-migrator-offset` header, which holds the source offset, and moves to the exact record. For a group with active members, it stops at the timestamp lookup, which can land a few records early where several records on a partition share a millisecond timestamp, so a consumer that moves while its group is still active can read those records again. The migrator never moves a target offset backwards. So:

- Stop every consumer of a group before you wait for its offsets, so the group is `Empty` and its translation is exact, and keep consumers idempotent, or deduplicating by key, across the cutover anyway.
- Repoint a producer only after the migrator's lag on its topics is 0, so that no record written directly to the target precedes a migrated record with the same key.

Three source conditions need a test of their own before the cutover, on a copy of the real topics:

- **Transactional producers and read_committed consumers.** The input here uses `transaction_isolation_level: read_committed`, so it copies only committed records and skips aborted ones, and the target never sees the transaction markers. Each commit or abort marker on the source takes an offset that has no record on the target, so offsets drift further apart. A read_committed consumer usually commits an offset just after a commit marker, and the migrator reads the record just before the committed offset to translate it. Check what happens on your topics: watch `redpanda_migrator_cg_offset_translation_errors_total` for each group, compare the records the source and target offsets point at with `scripts/compare-offsets.sh`, and move a test group before a real one. The output has no transactional setting and writes copied records outside any transaction, so a read_committed consumer on the target reads every copied record.
- **Trimmed log starts.** Retention or `DeleteRecords` moves the source's log start offset, as here. The migrator copies from the log start, so the target starts at 0. A group whose committed offset is at or below the source's log start offset is skipped (there is no earlier record to translate from), and a consumer of that group starts on the target from its `auto.offset.reset` policy. Find such groups with `rpk group describe` before the cutover.
- **Compaction gaps.** A compacted source topic has offsets with no record, and the target copy has none, so offsets differ there too. If the record just before a committed offset was compacted away, the migrator cannot read it to translate that offset. Count the translation errors per group, and compare the record each offset points at rather than the offset numbers.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/).

### Dead-letter handling

In this solution, there is no dead-letter topic: a record the migrator cannot write is retried, and the pipeline stops on a permanent error.

In production, keep that behavior, since a migration that drops records is not a migration. Alert on `output_error` and on a rising `redpanda_lag`, fix the cause (usually a missing ACL or a full disk on the target), and keep the source until the target has been verified.

See [Error Handling](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/configuration/error_handling/).

### Observability

In this solution, `make lag` reads the migrator's Prometheus endpoint, and each cluster has its own Redpanda Console.

In production, scrape the migrator's `/metrics` (`redpanda_lag` and the `redpanda_migrator_*` counters) and both clusters into your monitoring. Alert when lag stays above a bound you set, the produce rate times the delay you accept, as `scripts/lag.sh --check` does with `LAG_BOUND`, and when any `redpanda_migrator_*_errors_total` counter moves, including `redpanda_migrator_cg_offset_translation_errors_total`.

See [Monitoring](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/guides/monitoring/) and [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/).

### Disaster recovery

In this solution, there is no standby: the source is the only other copy, and it is retired after the cutover.

In production, set up Shadowing after the migration so that a second Redpanda cluster stays level with the target, including consumer group offsets and schemas, and can take over if the target fails. The disaster recovery solution, [Survive a cluster outage without reconfiguring clients](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/), builds that setup end to end.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

In this solution, nothing reads the migrated topics except `orders-service`.

In production, enable Iceberg topics on the migrated topics that analytics needs, so the brokers write each record to an Iceberg table with no extra pipeline to run.

See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

## Reference build

How the reference system proves itself. Everything in this section belongs to that system (its seeded data, fixed counts, and local stack): use it to see what each rule protects, not as checks to copy into the target.

### Acceptance checks of the reference

The assertions `make verify` makes against the running reference system.

1. Both clusters answer, and the target reports healthy. Apache Kafka has no health endpoint in the Kafka API, so the source check is a metadata request. Retried because a cluster can be slow to answer for a few seconds after the cutover moves the consumers, with nothing wrong.
2. Authentication is enforced on the source: without credentials, the Kafka listener and the Schema Registry reject the request. (env -u strips the helper's RPK_* credentials.)
3. Least privilege: the migrator can read the source but not write to it, and can create only shop.* topics on the target. --acks 1 turns off the idempotent producer, so the write reaches the topic ACL check instead of stopping at the cluster-level producer ID request.
4. Every topic exists on the target with the same partition count and the same cleanup policy and retention.
5. Every record the source still holds is on the target: the number of records per topic (high watermark minus log start offset) is equal. The offsets themselves are not: the source's shop.orders log starts after 1,200 trimmed records, and the target's copy starts at 0. The producer has stopped by now; the retry covers the migrator's last batch.
6. Schemas: the same subjects, versions, and IDs on both registries, and shop.orders-value has the version registered after the migrator started.
7. Consumer group: orders-service has committed offsets on every source partition, the consumer that moved to the target has caught up there, and on every partition the first record it processed on the target is the record at the source's committed offset, which stands still since make stop-consumer. A consumer that started from earliest, or a translation that landed on another record, shows up as a mismatch.
8. The target Schema Registry is back in READWRITE mode.

### Failure modes of the reference

#### Start the environment

If `make up` stops with a container marked `unhealthy`, run `scripts/stack logs <service>`. The usual causes are less than 6 GB of memory available to Docker and a host port already in use. To move a port, change its `*_PORT` variable in `.env`, run `make up` again, and use the new port in the Console and migrator URLs. If a helper or Schema Registry reports `SASL authentication failed`, a data volume holds a user from an earlier run with a different password: `make clean` and start again. On Kubernetes, if `make k8s-up` times out, `kubectl -n kafka-migration get pods` shows which pod is not ready, and `kubectl -n kafka-migration describe redpanda target` shows why the target is not `Ready`.

#### Seed the source cluster

If a subject is missing, run `make schemas` again: registering the same schema twice returns the same ID. If `rpk topic create` reports `TOPIC_ALREADY_EXISTS` for a topic whose partition count differs from the four topics table, you created that topic earlier with other settings. Delete it with `scripts/stack exec rpk-source rpk topic delete <name>`, then run `make topics` again, and `make history` too if the topic was `shop.orders`. If `make history` printed a table where the high watermark is above the log start offset, the topic already held records when it ran, and it skipped the trim: start over with `make clean`.

#### Start the shop's workload

The group is `Stable` with one member; the lag is whatever the service has not read in the last second. If the state is `Empty` or the group does not exist, the service could not connect: `scripts/stack logs orders-consumer` shows whether it was authentication (a changed password in `.env` after the first `make up`) or a missing topic (`make topics` first). If the producer logs `schema for shop.orders-value not found`, run `make schemas`.

#### Grant the migrator least-privilege access

Five ACLs on the source: `READ` and `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on the `shop.` prefix, `READ` on the `redpanda-migrator` group, `DESCRIBE` on the `orders-service` group, and `DESCRIBE` on the cluster. The script grants the group ACLs once per group you name after the side (`orders-service` when you name none), so a real migration lists every group it moves. If the list is empty, the user was created but the script did not run. Run `scripts/stack exec rpk-source /scripts/migrator-acls.sh source`; if it reports `permission denied`, run `chmod +x scripts/*` first. If `rpk registry mode set` refused `IMPORT`, the target registry already holds a schema from an earlier attempt. Run `make clean` and repeat the steps from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/start-environment/), because `make clean` deletes the data of both clusters.

#### Start the migration

The first three of the twelve partitions on the target's `shop.orders`, each with records already and a `LOG-START-OFFSET` of 0, where the same partitions on Kafka start at the offsets `make history` printed. If the topics do not appear, `scripts/stack logs migrator` shows the cause: `SASL authentication failed` means [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/) did not run on one side; `TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED` on `create topic` means the `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` grant is missing on the source; a registry error mentioning `IMPORT` means the target registry is not in `IMPORT` mode.

#### Verify the schemas

The record is the one `make schema-v2` produced on the source, copied by the migrator with its five-byte prefix unchanged. Both waiting commands poll until the record or version arrives. If one is still waiting after a minute, stop it with `Ctrl+C` and run `scripts/stack logs migrator | grep "Schema migration"` to see why; the usual cause is a target registry no longer in `IMPORT` mode (someone ran `make sr-readwrite` early), in which case the fixed-ID registration is refused.

#### Monitor the migration lag

The samples change on every run; the last line names the highest and the bound, and the script exits 1 when any sample is above it. The bound is `LAG_BOUND` in the environment. The script and the bound are under *Files for this step*. If the check fails, the migrator is not keeping up or has stopped writing: `scripts/stack logs migrator` shows the write error, such as an authorization failure on the target. If it reports that the migrator is not answering, `make migrate` did not start it.

#### Finish the cutover

The group is `Stable` with one member and `TOTAL-LAG 0`: the consumer is on the target and has read everything the migrator delivered. If `wait-offsets` times out, it prints the comparison table, and `scripts/stack logs migrator | grep "Consumer group"` shows why: `TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED` on `update offset` means the target grant is missing `READ` on `shop.`, and `failed to translate offset` means the migrator could not read the record before a committed offset. If `scripts/resumed.sh` shows `no` on a partition, the target consumer started before the offsets arrived and read from `earliest`, and its own commits now stand in the way of the translated ones: run `make clean` and repeat the solution, letting `make wait-offsets` finish before `make consumer-target`.

#### Verify end to end

A failed check names what it compared. The likely ones: `the same number of records` fails while the producer is still running (finish [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/) first), `mode is READWRITE` fails if you skipped `make sr-readwrite`, and `started on the record the source consumer would have read next` fails when the target consumer started before `make wait-offsets` finished.

## The problem

A Kafka cluster carries a shop's order flow: a Go service produces, a consumer group processes every order, and Schema Registry holds the contracts. Moving to Redpanda cannot mean stopping producers, replaying history, or losing where each consumer left off.

Redpanda Migrator copies topics, records, schemas, and offsets while the application writes. The consumer moves by changing two connection settings and resumes on the record it would have read next, although that record's offset differs on Redpanda.

**Note:** [Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/) is the recommended way to migrate from Kafka to Redpanda: a shadow link inside the target keeps every record at its source offset, so consumers move with their committed offsets untranslated. Use this Redpanda Migrator solution only when Shadowing cannot migrate your workload: the cluster you migrate to cannot run Shadowing (a version before 25.3, or no Enterprise Edition license), the source accepts only IAM or OAUTHBEARER authentication, your rollback plan needs records copied back to Kafka, or records must be renamed, filtered, or transformed on the way.

## What the system must do

- Move a live, SASL-secured cluster's topics, records, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda continuously, with a migration user that holds least-privilege ACLs on both clusters
- Keep schema IDs identical so that records already on the wire decode on the new cluster, including schemas registered mid-migration
- Read migration lag from the migrator's metrics and know when the target has caught up
- Cut a consumer group over to Redpanda from translated offsets by changing only its connection settings, then return the target Schema Registry to normal operation
- Prove the migration with exact assertions: partitions, configurations, record counts, schema IDs, and the record each consumer resumes on

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Turn on authentication on both clusters before either accepts its first connection, and name the cluster in every command so no command can reach the wrong side. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/start-environment/))
2. Before you migrate, inventory every topic's partition count, cleanup policy, and retention and every subject's schema IDs, because those are what a migration silently breaks, and keep partition counts unchanged until every consumer has moved. (from [Seed the source cluster](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/seed-source/))
3. Migrate underneath the running application, treat each consumer group's committed offsets as its record of what it has processed, and move clients by changing only their connection settings. (from [Start the shop's workload](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/start-workload/))
4. Run the migration tool as its own user with read-only ACLs on the source and prefixed create and write ACLs on the target, including `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on source topics and `READ` on target topics, and put the target Schema Registry in `IMPORT` mode before any schema reaches it. (from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/))
5. Move records, topic configurations, schemas, and consumer group offsets with one pipeline while the application keeps writing, keep schema IDs untranslated, and sync group offsets often enough that the cutover waits seconds. (from [Start the migration](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/start-migrator/))
6. Preserve every schema's ID and version on the target and sync the registry more often than schemas change, so copied records decode there and a schema registered mid-migration arrives before a record that uses it. (from [Verify the schemas](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-schemas/))
7. Gate the cutover on observable conditions, migration lag within a stated bound while traffic runs and at zero before a producer moves, and translated offsets that point at the same records as the source's, and watch the error counters as the audit trail. (from [Monitor the migration lag](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/monitor-lag/))
8. Cut over one consumer group at a time: stop the consumer, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets, and start it on the target; then pause the producer, drain to lag 0, and repoint it, which is the point of no return, and switch the target registry to `READWRITE` only after that. (from [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/))
9. Accept a migration only when the two clusters agree as compared from outside, on topic shapes, record counts, schema IDs, the records each consumer group resumes on, and security posture, including checks that forbidden requests are refused, and never on offset numbers being equal. (from [Verify end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

The cluster you leave is Apache Kafka: one KRaft node (`source`) with Confluent Schema Registry (`source-registry`). The cluster you move to is a single Redpanda broker (`target`). Both run SASL/SCRAM authentication and ACLs from the first boot. The shop's application, a Go producer and the `orders-service` consumer group built on the franz-go Kafka client, works against Kafka the whole time. Redpanda Migrator copies everything to Redpanda, and at the end you move the consumer.

- **`source` and `source-registry`**: four `shop.*` topics with different partition counts and cleanup policies, four Avro subjects, and the `orders-service` consumer group. The `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 records that retention already removed, as on a cluster that has run for months, so its offsets do not start at 0.
- **`producer`**: a Go service that writes one Avro record every 20 ms to the four topics, in the Schema Registry wire format with the IDs from the source registry.
- **`orders-consumer`**: the Go service `orders-service`, a consumer group on `shop.orders` that commits offsets every second. The same image later runs against the target with only its connection variables changed.
- **`migrator`**: the `redpanda_migrator` input and output, authenticated as the `migrator` user with read-only ACLs on the source cluster and write ACLs on the target only for `shop.*`. The source Schema Registry has no authorization here, so the same user could write there.
- **`target`**: receives the topics with their configurations, every record with its timestamp and schema ID, every schema with its ID, and the translated offsets of `orders-service`. Its copy of `shop.orders` starts at offset 0, so the same record has a different offset on each cluster.
- **Redpanda Console**, one per cluster, signed in as the superuser.

### Data flow

Left to right: the producer looks up the ID of each topic's schema in the Confluent Schema Registry and writes Avro records to the four `shop.*` topics on Kafka; the `orders-service` group consumes `shop.orders` and commits offsets to `__consumer_offsets`.

Redpanda Migrator reads the topics through the Kafka API as the `migrator` user, reads the registry over HTTP with the same user, and periodically reads the committed offsets of every consumer group on those topics. On the target it creates each topic with the source's partition count and configuration, produces every record with its original key, headers, timestamp, and schema ID, plus two headers of its own (`redpanda-migrator-offset` with the source offset and `redpanda-migrator-provenance` with the source cluster's ID), registers every schema version under its original ID, and commits the translated offsets for `orders-service`. The target registry runs in `IMPORT` mode until the cutover so that every schema keeps its original ID.

At the cutover the consumer stops on the source, the migrator's next sync commits target offsets that point at the same records as the source's, and the same `orders-service` image starts on the target and continues from there, with no code change.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A migration that cannot stop the business has three hard requirements. The applications must move without a rewrite. Every record must keep meaning the same thing, which for Avro means keeping its schema ID. And every consumer must resume at the record it would have read next, not at an offset number that means something else on the new cluster. Redpanda meets each of these:

- **Your clients move as they are.** Redpanda speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the shop's services, stock franz-go clients, keep their consumer groups, keyed partitioning, compaction, and Avro wire format, and the cutover changes `BROKERS` and `SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL` and nothing else. See [Kafka Compatibility](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/kafka-clients/).
- **Records, schemas, and consumer group offsets move in one pipeline.** Redpanda Migrator copies all three. MirrorMaker 2 copies records and offsets but not schemas, so a Kafka-to-Kafka migration usually runs a second tool for the registry. The migrator also adds the source offset to every copied record, which lets it translate the offset of a group with no active members (`Empty`) to the exact record even when offsets differ between the clusters. See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/).
- **Schema IDs survive.** The target's Schema Registry is part of the broker, and its `IMPORT` mode lets the migrator keep every schema ID, so records already on the wire decode on the target unchanged. See [Redpanda Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/).
- **One tool on both sides.** The `rpk` CLI reads topics, consumer groups, ACLs, and schemas on Apache Kafka and Confluent Schema Registry as well as on Redpanda, so each inventory and comparison in this solution is the same command against either cluster. Only SCRAM user management on Kafka uses the Kafka CLI. See [rpk Commands](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/).

## Acceptance

The target is done when every rule holds and you can cite the evidence from the target itself: a configuration value, a code path, a test, or a measured result. The reference build's numbers do not transfer.

- [ ] Rule 1 holds (Start the environment).
- [ ] Rule 2 holds (Seed the source cluster).
- [ ] Rule 3 holds (Start the shop's workload).
- [ ] Rule 4 holds (Grant the migrator least-privilege access).
- [ ] Rule 5 holds (Start the migration).
- [ ] Rule 6 holds (Verify the schemas).
- [ ] Rule 7 holds (Monitor the migration lag).
- [ ] Rule 8 holds (Finish the cutover).
- [ ] Rule 9 holds (Verify end to end).
- [ ] Every Adapt item is answered, and any rule that does not apply to the target is recorded with the reason.
