# Agent companion part 1 of 2: Survive a cluster outage without reconfiguring clients

Part 1 of 2 of the agent companion for the disaster-recovery solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Design contract

One entry per rule, in build order: the rule, where to look in the target, why the problem requires it, and what it depends on.

### 1. Start the environment

**Rule:** Run the recovery target as a separate, independently deployed cluster, and put the client-routing proxy in front of both clusters from the first day, not during the incident.

**Adapt:** Find the recovery cluster and how clients reach the primary; check that the two share no brokers or failure domain and whether clients connect through one stable address or a hard-coded broker list.

**The problem.** A recovery plan needs a second cluster that survives whatever takes out the first, and a way for clients to reach it. A copy on the same cluster goes down with it, and a proxy introduced during an incident is a change made under pressure.

**How Redpanda helps.** The two clusters are separate Redpanda deployments, not two brokers of one cluster, so stopping one leaves the other running. Shadowing is part of the broker: the only cluster property it needs is `enable_shadow_linking=true`, which this stack sets on both clusters, and the link you create next runs inside the shadow cluster, so there is no replication service to deploy. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

Envoy starts in front of both clusters from the beginning, before there is anything to fail over to, and each cluster already has the listener that advertises Envoy's address. A proxy that has been the only address clients know since the first day is the reason the incident is short.

**Other ways to do this.**

- A stretched cluster across regions: no acknowledged write is lost when one region fails, but every write waits on a cross-region round trip, and an event that takes out the whole cluster leaves no independent copy.
- MirrorMaker 2 between two clusters: it works between any Kafka-compatible clusters, but it is a separate set of workers to run, and it gives the copied records new offsets.

**In production:** Deploy, secure, and size the two clusters separately, in separate failure domains, so that one failure cannot take out both. Size the shadow cluster for the source's full throughput plus the replication catch-up.
Give every broker of both clusters a listener that advertises the proxy's address for that broker, fail all of a cluster's brokers over together, run the proxy as a highly available tier, and change the proxy before the old primary restarts.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: brokers and replication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-brokers-and-replication) and [client routing](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-client-routing).

### 2. Create the shadow link

**Rule:** Replicate consumer group offsets along with the records, scope the link's topic and group filters to a named prefix instead of `*`, and start a new link at the earliest offset.

**Adapt:** Find the replication configuration; check whether it carries consumer group offsets, what its topic and group filters match, and where a new link starts reading.

**The problem.** Copying the records is not enough to recover. Without the consumer groups' committed offsets, their bookmarks, every group that reconnects to the recovery cluster starts at the beginning of the topic or at the end, and both are wrong. A group that reprocesses a day of orders is an incident of its own. A group that skips to the end loses the records written between the last commit and the outage.

**How Redpanda helps.** One shadow link configuration carries the topic filters, the consumer group filters, and where replication starts. The recovery scope is one file you review and version, instead of settings spread across separate tools. Its consumer offset block replicates committed offsets along with the records, and that block is the part of the file that turns replication into recovery. See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [rpk shadow create](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-shadow/rpk-shadow-create/).

The filters use a prefix rather than `*` on purpose, which makes the recovery scope an explicit decision. The `start_at_earliest` option replicates each topic from its first offset, not from the moment you created the link. That is what you want when you add a link to a cluster that has been running for months.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Filters of `*` for every topic and group: nothing is left out by mistake, but the recovery cluster stores and replicates every topic, including topics nobody would fail over, and `rpk shadow failover --all` promotes all of them.
- Starting the link at the latest offset: the link has less to copy, but records written before the link existed never reach the recovery cluster.
- MirrorMaker 2 with its checkpoint connector: it also carries consumer offsets, but the copied records get new offsets on the target, so it translates each group's position through an offset mapping. A translated offset can land before where the group stopped, so the group can reprocess some records. Its scope also lives in a separate set of Kafka Connect workers instead of the link.

**In production:** Give the link TLS and credentials that can read only the topics and groups it replicates, and turn on authentication on both clusters and between clients and the proxy.
Replicate the Schema Registry on the same link when your records carry schema IDs, and enable schema ID validation on the promoted topics.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: security](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-security) and [schema validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-schema-validation).

### 3. Produce and consume the orders through Envoy, then prove parity

**Rule:** Prove replication parity before you need it by comparing both clusters' high watermarks partition by partition, check replicated consumer offsets separately, and treat the replication lag just before a failure as your recovery point.

**Adapt:** Find how replication health is monitored; check whether it compares per-partition watermarks on both clusters instead of trusting the link's own lag, and whether consumer offset lag is watched separately.

**The problem.** A recovery plan rests on one claim: the other cluster holds your records. That is a claim you check before you need it, not after. A total that does not match does not say which partition is behind. Under load, a total that matches is not proof either, because you read the two clusters at different moments, so one partition can be behind while another has caught up. And how far the copy trails the source decides your recovery point objective (RPO), how much recent data you can afford to lose.

**How Redpanda helps.** The shadow topic preserves the source's offsets, so partition 1 offset 5 is the same record on both clusters, and the replicated committed offsets need no translation. That is what makes a consumer's resume point portable. It is also why `make parity` can compare raw high watermarks, partition by partition, and mean something. Lag reported by the link is a good signal, but `make parity` asks the two clusters instead of asking the link about itself. See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/) and [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

The consumer offsets are checked separately, in the Verify section, because they travel on a different task of the same link and can lag behind the records. A recovery whose offsets trail the records still works. It just costs you a reprocessing run that nobody planned for, because the group resumes from an older commit.

Replication lag is also your recovery point. Shadowing replicates asynchronously, so the records the link has not fetched when the source fails are the records you lose. The `LAG` column in the `make status` output is that number per partition. Here it is 0, because nothing produces after `make parity`. Under real load it is rarely 0, so the reading that matters is the one taken just before the failure, which the next step measures under a running producer. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/).

**Other ways to do this.**

- Trusting the lag the link reports: it is cheap to watch, but it is the link describing itself, not the two clusters confirming they hold the same records.
- Synchronous replication, such as a stretched cluster across regions: no acknowledged write is lost when one region fails, but every write waits on a round trip to another region.
- Envoy's Kafka broker filter (`envoy.filters.network.kafka_broker`, in the `contrib` image) instead of proxy listeners on the brokers: it rewrites broker addresses in Metadata responses, so the brokers need no extra listener. It decodes only the request versions it was built with and closes a connection it cannot decode, so you pin clients to old request versions.

**In production:** Monitor parity and consumer offset lag continuously and alert on them, because that alert is what tells you whether a failover is safe on the day.
Set a replication lag threshold from the data you can afford to lose and alert on it, measure the recovery point under live writes, and measure the recovery time in every rehearsal, including the decision to promote.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: observability](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-observability) and [recovery point and recovery time](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-recovery-point-and-time).

### 4. Simulate the disaster

**Rule:** Rehearse the outage as an ungraceful kill under live writes and commits, let the proxy move clients for reads automatically, keep shadow topics read-only until a person promotes them, and decide in advance what happens to the writes refused in that window.

**Adapt:** Find how clients react to losing the primary cluster; check whether reaching the other cluster needs a config change or a redeploy, whether DR tests stop the primary gracefully or kill it, and what producers do with a refused write.

**The problem.** When the primary cluster goes down, clients have to reach the other one. If that means editing a bootstrap server list, redeploying an application, or updating a DNS record, someone does it under pressure, in the middle of the outage. Writes are harder. If the recovery cluster accepted writes and the source cluster came back, two clusters would hold writes to the same partitions with no way to reconcile them. And a rehearsal that stops the primary politely, with nothing writing, proves neither: a real outage arrives mid-write, and the records in flight are the ones you lose.

**How Redpanda helps.** A shadow topic refuses produce requests for as long as the link considers it a replica. That read-only state is what makes it safe to move clients before you promote anything: the worst the proxy can do is send a producer to a cluster that refuses it, and refusing is the correct answer until a person decides the source is not coming back. The records were already on the shadow cluster, so the outage costs a reconnect rather than a change-management process. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/).

The streaming consumer stops reading as soon as Envoy routes to the shadow cluster, the way a runbook pauses a replicated group's consumers until the promotion: the [Shadowing setup guide](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) warns that a group consuming on the shadow cluster under the same name interferes with the offsets the link replicates. The `observer-during-disaster` group in step 3 does not start with `dr-`, so it has no replicated offsets and reads from the beginning, which shows that the records are all present independently of any bookmark.

**Other ways to do this.**

- DNS failover: there is no extra component in the data path, but the move waits on record TTLs, on the DNS caches in the operating system and the client runtime, and on each Kafka client going back to its bootstrap address, which it does only when every broker it knows is unreachable.
- Letting the recovery cluster accept writes as soon as clients arrive: writes resume sooner, but if the source comes back, both clusters hold writes to the same partitions that cannot be reconciled.

**In production:** Decide in advance what happens to the writes the shadow cluster refuses between the outage and the promotion: buffer them, dead-letter them, or accept the loss explicitly.
Use idempotent producers and a written cut-over order. For a planned failover or a failback, stop the producers, wait for lag to reach zero, fail over, then restart the producers against the new primary; in an outage, decide in advance to accept the lag at failure as lost.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: dead-letter handling](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-dead-letter-handling) and [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery).

### 5. Fail the shadow topics over

**Rule:** Keep promotion a separate, manual, irreversible step from the client move, taken only once someone decides the source cluster is gone for good, and time it in every rehearsal.

**Adapt:** Find the failover runbook and any automation that promotes the recovery cluster; check who authorizes promotion, whether a short outage can trigger it, and whether its duration is recorded.

**The problem.** Moving clients and promoting the recovery cluster answer different questions. A proxy answers "which cluster can serve this connection" automatically, in seconds, and reversibly. Nothing answers "is the source cluster gone for good" automatically: a cluster that is unreachable for thirty seconds during a network event must not be replaced, and a proxy cannot tell the difference. Automatic promotion would let that blip become a split brain, with two clusters accepting writes.

**How Redpanda helps.** Promotion is a separate, manual `rpk shadow failover` command, and it is a state change, not a copy. The data is already in the shadow topic's partitions at the source's offsets, so failing over six partitions across two topics is quick. The report times it, from `rpk shadow failover` to every topic reporting `FAILED_OVER`. Each partition stops its replication fetcher and starts accepting produce requests, and the next record is appended at the offset after the last replicated one. The consumer group's committed offsets are already in the shadow cluster's `__consumer_offsets`, so the group resumes without being told anything. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/) and [rpk shadow failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-shadow/rpk-shadow-failover/).

Once the topics are promoted the link stops fetching, so the shadow cluster is no longer tracking the source. If the source cluster came back now, its records after the last replicated offset would exist nowhere on the shadow cluster, and the two logs would have diverged. That is why promotion comes after the client move, not with it.

Promotion also cannot be undone: a failed-over topic cannot return to shadow mode, and there is no automatic failback to the source cluster. Failing back is a planned operation of its own, with a reverse link and a maintenance window, which [Fail back to the old primary](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#fail-back-to-the-old-primary) walks through.

This step also ends the recovery time objective (RTO) clock, the measure of how long recovery takes. Reads came back when Envoy moved clients in the previous step, but writes come back only now. For writes, the recovery time runs from the outage to the first write the shadow cluster accepts. In an incident it covers the time for Envoy to move clients, the time to decide, and the time to promote the shadow topics; the report measures only the machine time. Record those numbers in each rehearsal, as the [failover runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/) asks.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Promoting automatically when health checks fail: the write outage is shorter, but a short network event can promote the recovery cluster while the source is still alive, and the two logs diverge.
- A stretched cluster across regions that elects new leaders on its own: there is no promotion step, but every acknowledged write waits on a cross-region round trip. It is also still one cluster, so an event that affects the whole cluster, such as losing a majority of its regions, leaves no independent copy to fail over to.

**In production:** Keep the link configuration and the cluster manifests in version control, rehearse the failover runbook on a schedule, and plan the failback before you need it.
Give every broker of both clusters a listener that advertises the proxy's address for that broker, fail all of a cluster's brokers over together, run the proxy as a highly available tier, and change the proxy before the old primary restarts.
For the full picture, see [Production considerations: disaster recovery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-disaster-recovery) and [client routing](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-client-routing).

### 6. Verify the recovery end to end

**Rule:** Record each claim at the moment you measure it, because parity before an outage cannot be measured after it, and verify a recovery with exact equalities on watermarks, committed offsets, and topic state in a scheduled rehearsal.

**Adapt:** Find the disaster recovery tests or rehearsals; check whether they record pre-outage parity when it is true and assert exact offsets and group resume points rather than estimates.

**The problem.** A recovery you cannot verify is a recovery you have to take on trust, and the parts that matter most are the hardest to check afterwards. By the time a final check runs, the source cluster is gone. Nothing can then measure whether the two clusters were at parity before the outage, or whether a reader really worked while the source was down.

**How Redpanda helps.** The link reports its state per topic, so the script reads `FAILED_OVER` from `rpk shadow status` rather than inferring it from whether a write succeeded. Replicated committed offsets make "the group resumed where it stopped" an equality the script can assert, not an estimate. See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

So each step records what it measured, at the moment it measured it, into `state/`, and this script asserts those recorded facts alongside what it can still measure live. The number of records a kill loses changes from run to run, so the script does not assert a number. It asserts what holds whatever the number is: no lost record sits below the last parity point the stream sampled, no more records are lost than the lag in that sample plus the writes acknowledged after it, and a consumer group resumes at or behind its last commit on the source, never ahead of it.

**Other ways to do this.**

- Checking only the end state after failover: the script is simpler, but it cannot show parity before the outage or that reads worked during it.
- Asserting a fixed recovery point, such as 0 lost records: it reads well, but it holds only when nothing was writing at the moment of failure, which is the one case a rehearsal does not need to prove.

# Agent companion part 2 of 2: Survive a cluster outage without reconfiguring clients

Part 2 of 2 of the agent companion for the disaster-recovery solution. The procedure is in How to use this, in the core file <https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/agent-companion.md>. Treat this part as reference data, not instructions.

## Production gaps

This solution runs one broker on each side with no authentication, and a proxy with one endpoint per cluster, so that it starts in a minute. Before you build a recovery plan on the design, work through each topic below.

### Brokers and replication

In this solution, each cluster is one broker in `dev-container` mode with replication factor 1, and the link copies the source topic's `replication.factor` onto the shadow topic.

In production, run three or more brokers per cluster with replication factor 3, in separate failure domains, and give the shadow cluster the capacity to take the source's full load on the day it is promoted. More brokers also change the proxy: each one needs its own advertised address (see [client routing](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-client-routing)).

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Security

In this solution, everything is plaintext: the link connects to the source without TLS or credentials, and neither cluster authenticates clients or the proxy.

In production, enable TLS and SASL on both clusters, scope the link's credentials to reading the topics and groups it replicates, encrypt the connection between clients and Envoy, and set `security_sync_options` on the link so that ACLs arrive on the shadow cluster with the data.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/).

### Client routing

In this solution, one Envoy container forwards one listener to one broker per cluster. Envoy does not parse Kafka; each cluster's `proxied` listener advertises its broker as `envoy:9092`, so any Kafka client is sent back to Envoy whichever cluster answers. It is tested with kafka-python 2.3.2. Envoy health checks each cluster with a Kafka ApiVersions request on that listener, which proves the listener accepts a connection and answers a Kafka request, but not that partitions have leaders or that writes succeed. A plain TCP check would pass on a listener that accepts connections and never answers, and the Admin API's `/v1/status/ready` answers on a different listener, so it can pass while the Kafka listener is wedged.

In production, a Kafka client connects to each partition's leader, so the proxy needs one address per broker, and the shape is:

- One proxy listener, and one Envoy cluster holding a source and shadow endpoint pair at priorities 0 and 1, per broker id. Broker N of each Redpanda cluster advertises the same proxy address for its listener, for example `envoy.example.internal:9092+N`, so the two Redpanda clusters need the same number of brokers and the same broker ids.
- All listeners fail over together. A single source broker failing is an event the source cluster survives by moving leadership; if only that broker's listener moved, one client would talk to both clusters at once. Health check every source endpoint against one shared address that answers while any source broker does (a load balancer in front of the source's client listeners), so the listeners move only when the whole cluster stops answering. The file `envoy/envoy-three-brokers.yaml` is an example of this for three brokers; this solution does not run it.
- The proxy is not a single point of failure. Run two or more Envoy instances with the same configuration behind a TCP load balancer or a DNS name. They make their health decisions independently and can disagree for a few seconds during an outage; that is safe for writes only because shadow topics refuse them until the promotion.

Without a proxy, give clients a DNS name or load balancer per broker and switch it at failover in the runbook. Envoy's Kafka broker filter can rewrite broker addresses in Metadata responses instead of relying on advertised listeners, but it decodes only the request versions it was built with and closes connections it cannot decode, so test your client's negotiated versions against it.

Envoy's priority list is symmetric: it sends clients back to the source as soon as the source passes its health checks again. Make the proxy change part of the failover runbook and do it before the old primary restarts, as the failback extension does with `envoy/envoy-promoted.yaml`. Shadowing has no automatic fallback, and the proxy must not add one.

See [Configure Listeners](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/listener-configuration/), [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/), and [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/).

### Partitions

In this solution, one topic has three partitions, and the link copies the source partition count onto the shadow topic.

In production, size the partitions on the source. Adding partitions to a source topic after the link exists adds them to the shadow topic too, and every consumer group has to cope with the change on both clusters.

See [Sizing Guidelines](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/sizing/).

### Schema validation

In this solution, the orders are plain JSON with no schema ID, so the link does not replicate the Schema Registry and neither broker validates records.

In production, add `schema_registry_sync_options` to the link: topic mode (`shadow_schema_registry_topic`) for a Redpanda source, API mode for a Confluent-compatible registry. After a failover, enable schema ID validation on the promoted topics so that a producer pointed at the new primary cannot write records the consumers cannot decode.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/).

### Consumer scaling

In this solution, one consumer instance in the `dr-consumers` group reads three partitions.

In production, scale each group on its lag, and size the shadow cluster for every group reconnecting and catching up at the same moment, not for the steady state.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Data retention

In this solution, the link starts at the earliest offset and syncs `retention.ms` and `segment.ms` from the source.

In production, keep the retention properties in the link's synced properties so the shadow topics match the source, and use Tiered Storage on the shadow cluster to make long retention affordable.

See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/).

### Compaction

In this solution, `dr-orders` uses the default delete policy, and the link syncs `cleanup.policy` along with the compaction properties, as the Synced Shadow Topic Properties list in `rpk shadow status` shows.

In production, check that every compacted topic in the link's filters keeps its `cleanup.policy` and compaction lag settings on the shadow cluster, because a consumer that rebuilds state from a compacted topic after a failover reads whatever the shadow cluster kept.

See [Compaction Settings](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/compaction-settings/).

### Idempotency and delivery

In this solution, the client produces with `acks=all` and no retries, so a failed write is visible rather than silently duplicated.

In production, enable idempotence and document the cut-over order. A producer that writes to both clusters during a failover produces records that no replication can reconcile.

See [Idempotent producers](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/produce-data/idempotent-producers/).

### Dead-letter handling

In this solution, nothing handles them. A write that the shadow topic refuses surfaces as a `PolicyViolationError` in the client, and the streaming producer only records each one in `state/stream-errors.jsonl`.

In production, buffer the producer's writes or send them to a dead-letter store during the window between the outage and the failover, and replay them once the promoted topics accept writes. Rehearse that window: it is the part of the plan that only shows up in an incident.

See [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/) and [Configure Producers](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/produce-data/configure-producers/).

### Observability

In this solution, you read `rpk shadow status`, `make parity`, `make offsets`, and Envoy's admin API by hand.

In production, alert on the link's lag and task states (the [recovery point and recovery time](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-recovery-point-and-time) topic lists the metrics), on Envoy's endpoint health and priority changes, and on the difference between the two clusters' high watermarks. A link whose lag grew unnoticed is not a recovery plan.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/) and [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/).

### Disaster recovery

In this solution, one link fails over once, in one direction, and the walkthrough stops there. The failback extension on the last step reverses it.

In production, follow the failover runbook, including the decision to fail over, who makes it, and the client cut-over. Plan the failback as its own operation, because a failover cannot be undone and the old primary's log diverged at the moment it failed:

1. Change the proxy, DNS, or load balancer so that clients prefer the promoted cluster, before the old primary starts again.
1. Rebuild the old primary empty, with topic auto-creation off, so that no client creates a topic there before the reverse link creates its shadow topic. Records it wrote after the last replicated offset exist nowhere else; recover them from the producers or accept their loss, but do not bring them back in place.
1. Delete the original link with `rpk shadow delete` once its topics are `FAILED_OVER`, and create a reverse link on the old primary that fetches from the promoted cluster, with the same filters and `start_at_earliest`.
1. Wait for parity on every partition and for the consumer group offsets, and keep watching the reverse link's lag until the window. A link that has not read the source yet reports no lag or `-1`, not 0, so do not read either as caught up.
1. In a maintenance window, stop the producers, check parity again and stop if it fails, switch the proxy back to the old primary while its topics are still read-only, run `rpk shadow failover` on the reverse link, and restart the producers.
1. Rebuild the other cluster empty and recreate the original link, so the primary is protected again.

Review the link's topic, group, and security filters whenever the recovery plan changes, and keep the link configuration and the cluster manifests in Git so that the recovery topology is reviewed like any other change. On Kubernetes, put the two clusters in two Kubernetes clusters in separate regions. Run this solution's verification as a scheduled rehearsal against a real pair of clusters, kill the primary rather than stopping it, and give the report to someone who reads it.

See [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/), [rpk shadow delete](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-shadow/rpk-shadow-delete/), [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/), and [Deploy Redpanda for Production in Kubernetes](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/kubernetes/k-production-deployment/).

### Recovery point and recovery time

In this solution, both clusters run on one machine, so the round trip between them is well under a millisecond. The `make recovery-report` target counts the acknowledged records a kill lost, the replication lag in the last sample before it, how far each streaming consumer group falls back, and the recovery times on that machine, with no decision time.

In production, treat the replication lag at the moment of failure as your recovery point, because Shadowing replicates asynchronously, and expect it to be larger across regions. Three things set a floor under it that no amount of capacity removes:

- The round trip between the regions. Every fetch the shadow cluster makes costs at least one, so records written within the last round trip are always at risk.
- The fetch wait. The link's fetcher waits up to `fetch_wait_max_ms` (500 ms by default) for `fetch_min_bytes` to accumulate, so at low throughput the shadow trails by up to that wait plus the round trip. Lower it for a tighter floor, at the cost of more fetch requests.
- The consumer offset sync interval. Committed offsets travel every `interval` under `consumer_offset_sync_options`, so a group can lose up to that interval of commits and reprocess those records after a failover, on top of the records lost from the topic.

Cross-region replication also costs egress: the source region pays for every byte the shadow cluster fetches, which `redpanda_shadow_link_total_bytes_fetched` measures. Size the link's scope with its filters for that bill.

Monitor these Shadowing metrics, and alert on:

- The lag metric, `redpanda_shadow_link_shadow_lag`, per `shadow_link_name`, `topic`, and `partition`: when it exceeds the records your RPO allows (your write rate times the seconds of data you can lose), or keeps growing without recovering.
- Client errors, `redpanda_shadow_link_client_errors`: when it rises quickly, which means the shadow cluster is struggling to reach the source.
- Topic states, `redpanda_shadow_link_shadow_topic_state` per `state`: when any topic is in `FAULTED`.
- Throughput, `redpanda_shadow_link_total_records_fetched` and `redpanda_shadow_link_total_bytes_fetched`: when they drop sharply while the source is still taking writes.
- The link's task states in `rpk shadow status`: when a task reports `FAULTED`, `NOT_RUNNING`, or `LINK_UNAVAILABLE`.

Record the recovery time for reads and for writes in each rehearsal, as the runbook asks; the time to decide usually dominates the write time.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/), [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/), and [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

In this solution, there is no analytics path.

In production, a shadow cluster is also a place to read the replicated data without loading the primary: Iceberg topics on the shadow cluster write it to a lakehouse table.

See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

## Reference build

How the reference system proves itself. Everything in this section belongs to that system (its seeded data, fixed counts, and local stack): use it to see what each rule protects, not as checks to copy into the target.

### Acceptance checks of the reference

The assertions `make verify` makes against the running reference system.

1. What is left standing: the source cluster is gone, everything else is up.
2. Before the disaster: the source cluster was the writer, reached through Envoy.
3. Before the disaster: replication was at parity, record for record.
4. Before the disaster: the group's committed offsets were replicated too.
5. During the disaster: the client kept working, with no configuration change.
6. After failover: the shadow topics are ordinary topics and accept writes.
7. After failover: the consumer resumed instead of reprocessing.
8. The recovery point and recovery time. How many records the kill lost
9. The end state on the shadow cluster: 12 replicated plus 6 new.
10. The Kubernetes manifests still describe the same clusters, images, and link

### Failure modes of the reference

#### Start the environment

Every service reports `healthy`, and Envoy routes clients to the source cluster. On Kubernetes, `make health` reports a Deployment as `healthy` when its pod is ready, and a cluster when its `Redpanda` resource is `Ready`. If a service is `unhealthy`, run `scripts/stack logs <service>` (`kubectl -n disaster-recovery logs redpanda-source-0` for a cluster on Kubernetes). The usual causes are less than 6 GB of memory available to Docker and a host port already in use. To move a port, change the matching `*_PORT` variable in `.env` and run `make up` again. On Kubernetes, change the `hostPort` in `kubernetes/kind.yaml` and recreate the kind cluster.

#### Create the shadow link

The `dr-orders` topic reports `State: ACTIVE`, which means the link is replicating it, and every partition's lag is `0` because there is nothing to replicate yet. The target waits up to two minutes for the link to report every partition before it prints. If `dr-orders` is missing, check that you created it on the source cluster. If you created it on the shadow cluster, delete it there with `scripts/stack exec rpk-shadow rpk topic delete dr-orders` and run `make topic` again. If the link itself is missing, `make link` failed; run it again and read its error, which is usually the source cluster not being reachable at `redpanda-source:9092`. On Kubernetes, `kubectl -n disaster-recovery describe shadowlink disaster-recovery` shows the error the Operator got.

#### Produce and consume the orders through Envoy, then prove parity

The offsets on the shadow cluster are the same numbers the group committed on the source. The script waits up to two minutes for them to match and prints nothing until they do. If it times out, it prints both clusters' offsets. A `None` on the shadow side means the link does not replicate the group: its ID must start with `dr-`, and the group here is `dr-consumers`.

#### Simulate the disaster

The `PolicyViolationError` here is the Kafka error a shadow topic returns for a produce request. If the write succeeds instead, the topics were already failed over and the six orders are now on the topic, which breaks the later counts: run `make clean` (`make k8s-clean` and then `make k8s-up` on Kubernetes) and start again. If the script waits about four minutes and prints `Envoy has no healthy cluster to send this client to`, the shadow cluster is unhealthy too; check it with `make health`.

#### Fail the shadow topics over

Six records, not 18: the group resumed from the offsets the link replicated instead of reprocessing the topic. If it reads 18 records, the offsets did not arrive before the failover, which means the group's id does not match the link's group filter. If it reads 0, the group was already advanced to the end of the topic by an earlier run; run `make clean` and start again (on Kubernetes, `make k8s-clean` and then `make k8s-up`).

In the shadow Console at http://localhost:8381, open **Consumer Groups**. The `dr-consumers` group now shows **Offset Lag (Sum)** 0: it just read the six records appended after the replicated offsets. Before `make consume-after-failover` it showed 6, the records it had not yet read on this cluster. The `observer-during-disaster` group is the one that read during the outage, without committing. The `dr-event-consumers` group is the workload's consumer from the previous step. The workload stopped during the outage, so this group keeps its lag: the records after the last commit the link replicated for it, a number that varies from run to run.

#### Verify the recovery end to end

The last line reads `PASS (31/31)`, and the script exits 0. A failed check names what it expected and what it got. A check that fails with `got ''` read a state file that does not exist, so its step was skipped: run `make clean`, then `make up` and `make seed`, which runs the whole path in order. On Kubernetes, run `make k8s-clean`, `make k8s-up`, and `make seed`.

## The problem

A shop writes every confirmed order to one topic, and a fulfillment consumer group ships from it. If that cluster goes away, two numbers decide the damage: orders lost (the recovery point) and how long fulfillment stops (the recovery time).

You build two Redpanda clusters joined by a shadow link, behind one Envoy address. You kill the primary under a live workload, fail over, and measure both numbers: the lost records, and the seconds until reads and writes resume.

## What the system must do

- Configure one shadow link that replicates a topic's records and a consumer group's committed offsets to a second cluster
- Prove parity partition by partition before you trust the link with a failover
- Route Kafka clients through Envoy so that a failover needs no change to the client's configuration
- Kill the primary under a running producer and consumer, and count the acknowledged records the failover lost and the records each consumer group processes again
- Fail shadow topics over, report the recovery times, and show that a consumer resumes from the replicated offsets instead of reprocessing the topic

The stack runs on Docker Compose or on Kubernetes, where the two clusters and the link are `Redpanda` and `ShadowLink` resources for the Redpanda Operator. [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/start-environment/) has a tab for each.

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Run the recovery target as a separate, independently deployed cluster, and put the client-routing proxy in front of both clusters from the first day, not during the incident. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/start-environment/))
2. Replicate consumer group offsets along with the records, scope the link's topic and group filters to a named prefix instead of `*`, and start a new link at the earliest offset. (from [Create the shadow link](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/create-shadow-link/))
3. Prove replication parity before you need it by comparing both clusters' high watermarks partition by partition, check replicated consumer offsets separately, and treat the replication lag just before a failure as your recovery point. (from [Produce and consume the orders through Envoy, then prove parity](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/route-clients-through-envoy/))
4. Rehearse the outage as an ungraceful kill under live writes and commits, let the proxy move clients for reads automatically, keep shadow topics read-only until a person promotes them, and decide in advance what happens to the writes refused in that window. (from [Simulate the disaster](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/simulate-disaster/))
5. Keep promotion a separate, manual, irreversible step from the client move, taken only once someone decides the source cluster is gone for good, and time it in every rehearsal. (from [Fail the shadow topics over](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/fail-over/))
6. Record each claim at the moment you measure it, because parity before an outage cannot be measured after it, and verify a recovery with exact equalities on watermarks, committed offsets, and topic state in a scheduled rehearsal. (from [Verify the recovery end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

Two single-broker Redpanda clusters with Shadowing enabled, one shadow link between them, and an Envoy proxy in front of both. A Python client plays the shop: it produces orders and reads them as the fulfillment consumer group, through Envoy, and it is never told that there are two clusters. You kill the source cluster while a second workload is still writing and committing, and the client reads every replicated record through the same address once Envoy moves it.

- **Source cluster** (`redpanda-source`): the cluster that serves clients until it fails.
- **Shadow cluster** (`redpanda-shadow`): the failover target. It runs the link, fetches from the source, and holds the replicated topics read-only until you promote them.
- **The shadow link `disaster-recovery`**: one configuration file that replicates every topic whose name starts with `dr-`, with its records (`topic_metadata_sync_options`), and the committed offsets of every consumer group whose ID starts with `dr-` (`consumer_offset_sync_options`).
- **Envoy**: the only Kafka endpoint clients are given, a TCP proxy that does not parse Kafka. Each cluster has a listener that advertises its broker as `envoy:9092`, so the metadata a client gets back always points it at Envoy, whichever cluster answered. Envoy health checks each cluster with a Kafka request and sends traffic to the source cluster while it answers and to the shadow cluster when it does not.
- **Python client**, built on kafka-python 2.3.2: the order-capture service and the fulfillment consumer. It produces 12 orders to `dr-orders`, reads them as the `dr-consumers` group, reads them again during the outage as a separate group that the link does not replicate, and resumes as `dr-consumers` after the failover to read only the new records. One bootstrap address throughout.
- **A live workload**, `scripts/stream.py` in the same client: a producer that writes `dr-order-events` 20 times a second and records every acknowledged offset, a consumer group that commits after every batch, and a sampler that reads both clusters' watermarks once a second. It runs while the source is killed, so the recovery point is counted rather than assumed.
- **Two Redpanda Consoles**, one per cluster: the source view is what you lose in the outage, and the shadow view is where you watch replication arrive.
- **Kubernetes manifests**: the same two clusters and the same link as `Redpanda` and `ShadowLink` resources for the Redpanda Operator, and every other service as a Deployment of the same name, for the Kubernetes path.

### Data flow

Left to right: the client holds one address, `envoy:9092`. Envoy forwards the connection, byte for byte, to the source cluster, its priority 0 endpoint. The source answers on a listener that advertises its broker as `envoy:9092`, so the client's next connection comes back to Envoy instead of going straight to a broker. Behind the clusters, the shadow link runs on the shadow cluster and pulls from the source. Its topic sync task creates a shadow topic for every source topic that matches the `dr-` filter and replicates its records from the first offset. Its consumer offset sync task copies the committed offsets of every group that matches the same prefix. While the link is active, the shadow topics reject writes.

When the source cluster stops answering, Envoy's health check fails and it moves traffic to its priority 1 endpoint, the shadow cluster, whose listener advertises the same `envoy:9092`. Reads resume on the same address as soon as the health checks fail the source, because the replicated records are already there; [Fail the shadow topics over](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/fail-over/) reports how long that took in your run, and how many acknowledged records the link had not copied yet. Writes are still refused, because a shadow topic is read-only by design: that is what stops both clusters accepting writes at once. The `rpk shadow failover` command promotes the shadow topics to ordinary topics, and from that point the same address serves reads and writes from the shadow cluster, with each consumer group resuming from the offset the link replicated.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A disaster recovery setup is only as good as its failover. A second cluster has to stay current without anyone watching it. Consumers have to resume where they left off, not reprocess the day or skip records. Nothing may write to the standby while the primary is still alive, or the two diverge. And the whole arrangement has to be simple enough to rehearse, because a failover nobody has practiced is a guess. Redpanda builds this into the broker with Shadowing:

- **One link for records and consumer offsets, in the broker.** Shadowing replicates the topics and the consumer group offsets from one configuration file, with no connector, no separate replication cluster, and no state store to operate: the destination cluster fetches from the source and reports its own lag. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).
- **Offsets preserved.** A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, so an offset a consumer committed on the source means the same record on the shadow, and a replicated commit needs no translation. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).
- **Read-only until you promote.** Shadow topics reject produce requests until you fail them over, so a proxy that moves clients early cannot cause a split brain, and the promotion is a separate, auditable step a person takes. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/).
- **The same link on Kubernetes.** The Redpanda Operator takes the link as a `ShadowLink` resource, so the recovery topology is part of the cluster's desired state. See [cluster.redpanda.com/v1alpha2](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/k-crd/).

Because the clients speak the Kafka API, they need no Redpanda-specific failover logic: the stock kafka-python clients here reconnect through Envoy, a TCP proxy that health-checks both clusters, to whichever one is serving, and resume from their group's committed offsets as on any Kafka cluster. If you run Kafka or Amazon MSK today, [Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) moves a live workload's topics, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda first.
